CONSTANTINOPLE, Oct. 8. When the Grand Council had resolved on war, there were difficulties in respect to the finances, the disposition of the troops, Ac. These difficulties were principally raised by Fehti-Achmet Pasha Ordnance). Riza Pasha (ex-Minister of War), and Fuad Effendi (ex-Minister of Foreign Affairs). At the next sitting (on the 26th), Redschid Pasha made a most remarkable speech, which put an end to all discussion. Ilis object was to show that Turkey, having done its utmost to preserve peace, had no choice left but to resolve on war, as the only means of maintaining the dignity and integrity of the Empire. The address was received with the greatest enthusiasm þÿ the Uleinahs and Hadjis, those faithful partisans of the war party, complimented the Minister, and expressed the warmest attachment to him. The Grand Scr:i' skier, Meheniet All Pasha, a chivalrous and generous character, who had always

opposed Redschid, not only forswore his aVicient enmity, hut declared that he would willingly lay down his life lor a man who had done so much for his country. It was a day of triumph, for Redschid, whose wise measures alone have placed Turkey in a position to wage war. The resolution of the Grand Council to declare war was submitted to the Sultan, who signed it. The contents of the document were then made known to the representatives of the four powers and to the Russian Chancellerie. Preparations are already made for the departure of this establishment (commercial), the Russian post, the interpreters, and all the subjects of the hostile power. However, if the Russian tradespeople choose to remain, they will not be exposed to molestation, and it is even proposed not to interrupt the mercantile navigation. The Austrian Internuncio, Bruck, required that no Polish or Magyar fugitive should be permitted to serve in the army in Rumelia (European Turkey), adding that should the request not j be complied with it would be considered an act ot hostility. The Porte consented, reserving, however, to itselfthe rijdit, under certain circumstances, of taking advantage of the services of the fugitives out of its Asiatic possessions. De la four declared that as France did not exactly approve ot the war, it would be out of her power to afford Turkey any active assistance. The reply of the Turkish minister was that the Emperor Napoleon III., the ruler of a great nation, was at liberty to fear Russia, but

that Turkey, in spite of the weakness attributed to her, would not hesitate when it was necessary to defend her rights and those of her sovereign. According to advices from Wallachia the movements ol the Russian troops indicate an intention to cross the Danube near \\ iddin. Messengers go to Rumclia and Anatolia to communicate to the commander ot the two provinces the resolve of the Grand Council, and the þÿSultan approval s of the same. On the 27th Lord Stratford was ad mitted to the presence of the Sultan, from whom he obtained a solemn promis» that war should not be declared before the 1st Moharrem (15th of October). A messenger was accordingly immediately despatched to Omcr Pasha, with positive instructions to abstain from all hostilities until that date, and to make known to Prince Gortsehakoff that such would be the case. New mirnrs (notes) are emitted. There i> a want of cash in ' nough is found for trade, State purposes. but money I he supplies are paid for in ready money, and the salaries and pensions arc not in arrears. The necessary sums are taken from the reserve funds. The treasury of the domains belonging to the mosques has not yet been touched, but, it necessary, it will be emptied without ceremony, the Sheickul-Islam having already given Ins consent. GT.OKGi: \VII>OV A few years since, as Mr. Gallaudet was walking in the streets of Hartford, there came running to him a poor bov, of very ordinary first-sight appearance, but whose fine, intelligent eye fixed the þÿgentleman sattention, as the bov inquired, þÿ Sir, can you tell me of a man who would like a boy to work for him, and learn to þÿread? þÿ Whose bov are you, and where do you live þÿ? þÿ I have no þÿparents, was the reply, þÿ and have just run away from the workhouse j because they would not teach me to þÿread. The gentleman made arrange | inents with the authorities of the town, and took the boy into his own family. There he learned to read. Nor was this all. He soon acquired the confidence of his new associates, by his faithfulness and honesty. He was allowed the use ot his þÿfriend s library, and made rapid progress in the acquisition ofknowledge. It became necessary, after a while, that George should leave Mr. Gallaudet, and he became apprenticed to a cabinet maker in the neighbourhood. There the same integrity won for him the favour of his new associates. To gratify his inclination for study, his master had a little room finished for him in the upper part of the shop, where he devoted his leisure time to his favourite pursuits. Here he made large attainments in mathematics in the French language, and other branches. After being in this situation a few years, as he sat at tea with the family one evening, lie all at once remarked that lie wanted to go to France. þÿ Go to France said his master, sur

prised that the apparently contented and dissatisfied happy youth, had thus suddenly become with his þÿsituation þÿ for þÿwhat? , þÿ Ask Mr. Gallaudet to tea to-morrow þÿevening, continued George, þÿ and I will þÿexplain. His kind friend was invited accordingly, and at tea-time the apprentice presented himself with Ins manuscripts, m English and French, and explained his singular intention to go to France. þÿ þÿ In the time of þÿNapoleon, said he, a prize was offered by the French government. for.the simplest rule for measuring plain surfaces, of whatever out line. The prize has never been awarded, and that method I have discovered." He then demonstrated his problem, to the surprise and gratification of his friends, who immediately furnished him with means of defraying his expenses, and with letters of introduction to Hon. Lewis Cass, then our Minister to the Court of France. He was introduced to Louis Philippe, and in the presence ol the king, nobles, and plenipotentiaries, this American youth demonstrated his problem, and received the plaudits ol the court, lie received the prize, which he had clearly won, besides valuable presents from the king. He then took letters of introduction, and proceeded to the Court of St. James, and took up a similar prize otfered by the Royal Society, and returned to the I nited States. Here he was preparing to secure the benefit ot his discovery by patent, when he received a letter from the Emperor Nicholas himself, one of whose ministers had witnessed his de-

monstrations at London, inviting him to make his residence at the Russian Court, and furnishing him with ample means for his outfit. He complied with the invitation, repaired to St. Petersburg!!, and is now Professor of Mathematics in the Royal College, under the special protection of the Autocrat of all the Russias !

Exaggerated Expressions. I was caught in the wet last night ; the rain came down in þÿtorrents. Most of us have been out in heavy rains; but a torrent of water pouring down from the skies would a little surprise us, after all. þÿ I am wet to the skin. I have not a single dry thread upon þÿme. Where these expressions are once used correctly, they are used twenty times in opposition to the truth. þÿ I went to the meeting, but had hard work to get in; for the place was crowded to þÿsuffocation. þÿ have I been sadly troubled with head-ache ; I thought I should have died, I was so þÿill. If they who use this expression on every light occasion did really reflect on death as frequently as they represent themselves to do so, it might be attended with the most salutary consequences. þÿ We came along the lane, a horrid road, up to our knees in þÿmud. Some people a little more diffident, satisfy themselves with saying, þÿ It was over my shoe-tops in þÿmud. All I can say is, that if either the one statement or the other be correct, it is high time the road should be mended. þÿ We stood there for an hour : my feet were as cold as þÿice. If the feet were once as cold as ice, there would be very little heat left in the head or the heart. þÿ must It have been a fine sight; I would have given the world to have seen þÿit. Fond as most of us are ot sight-seeing, this would be buying pleasure at a dear price indeed ; but it is an easy thing to proffer to part with that which we do not possess.

þÿ You þÿdon say t so ! why, it was enough to kill þÿhim! The fact that it did not kill him is a sufficient reply to this unfounded observation ; but no remark can be too absurd for an unbridled tongue. We are hearing continually the comparison, þÿ black as soot, white as snow, hot as fire, cold as ice, sharp as a needle, dull as a door-nail, light as a feather heavy as lead, stiff as a poker, and crooked as a þÿcrab-tree, in cases where such expressions are quite out of order.

Mr. Editor, Can you inform me if the extract of dog laws published in your paper of 1st lulv, refers to the dogs kept by the soldiers in the garrison? It seems not; as the soldiers are in the habit of enticing the dogs ofthe town into the Fort, where by some means they are accustomed and remain. These animals number some six or eight which exceeds that allowed in paragraph No. 2. Persons having business in the fort, are often attacked by these animals, in the presence of the sentry, who, instead of preventing them, urges them to it. Quite contrary to paragraph No. 3, these dogs are let out of the fort every night, with the sentry, who patrols about the

The Expected C omet of 1816. From an article published by ail eminent astronomer þÿ 111. Babinet, member þÿofl Academie des Sciences þÿ the French journals give us some interesting details relative to a comet which in all probability will appear sometime about the year 1856. This is one ofthe largest comets described by European or Chinese observers. Its periodical course is about three hundred years. It was seen in the years 104, 392, 682, 975, again in 1264, and the next time in 1556, always described as shining with an extraordinary brilliancy. Astronomers had agreed in announcing its return in 1848; but it has hitherto failed to appear, and, according to the quaint expression of M. Babinet, up to this moment is living on its brilliant reputation ! All the observatories were at first in despair regarding the fate of this beautiful star, and Sir John Herschell himself had put crape upon his telescope, when a wise calculator at Middleburg, M. Homme, had the good fortune to reassure the world that it was not lost to us, as had been feared, but only retarded in its motion. Anxious, as all others had been, at the nonarrival of this rare and renowned visitor, M. Bonime, aided by the preparatory J labors of Mr. Hind, with a patience anil devotedness truly Germau, went over the calculations, and made a new estimate of the separate and combined action of all the planets upon this comet, of three hundred years. The result of this severe labor gives its arrival in Au-

gust 1858, with an uncertainly of two years, more or less; so that between 1856 and 1860 we may hope to see that great luminary which in 1556 caused jected by reverses the result of the Charles V., to abdicate. Already de- þÿ siege of Metz þÿ the defeat of Rcntv the þÿ humiliation of the treaty of Passaw þÿ the combination of all these ' calamities drew þÿ from that monarch the despairing cry, Fortune abandons the þÿold! The appearance of the flaming meteor just at that time seemed, to his superstitious sense, a direct message from Heaven. Not that he thought it was directed towards himself as a man so much as to his station as a sovereign; and he abdicated the throne to save his life. It is well known how short a time lie survived in his monastic retiracy. Perhaps he might have lived longer had his superstition taken that better turn by which, in retaining power, he had directed his ambition towards a mote noble end. YVe know of no better use for comets than to point such a moral, and even theologians seldom find a higher interpretation of the celestial phenomena. þÿ American Paper.
Fear þÿol Ridicule. I know of no principle which it is of more importance to fix in the minds of young people, than that of the most de-

termined resistance to the encroachments of ridicule. Learn from your earliest days to inure your principles against the perils of ridicule. You can -no more exercise your reason if you live in constant dread of laughter, than you can enjoy your life if you are in constant terror of death. If you think it right to differ from the times, and to make a stand for any valuable point of morals, do it, however rustic, however antiquated, however pedantic it may appear ; do it, not for insolence, but seriously and grandly þÿ as a man who wore a soul of his own in his bosom, and did not wait till it was breathed into him by the breath of fashion. Let men call you mean, if you know you are just; hypocritical, if you are honestly religious; pusillanimous, if you feel that you are firm. Resistance soon converts unprincipled wit into sincere respect ; and no after time can tear from you those feelings which every man carries within him who has made a noble and successful exertion in a virtuous cause þÿ Sidney Smith.

A Sound Mind a Rare Thing. þÿ A perfectly just and sound mind is a rare and invaluable gift. It is given to but few, and a very small number of those few escape the influence of prejudice. i It is sometimes so strong as to destroy the judgment, and none are at all times perfectly free from its power. þÿ I once þÿsaw, says Mr. Cecil, þÿ this subject forcibly illustrated. A watchmaker told me, that a gentleman had put an exquisite watch into bis hands that went irregularly. It was as perfect a piece of work as was ever made, lie took it to pieces and put it together again twenty limes. No manner of defect was to be discovered, and yet the watch went intolerably. \t last it struck him, that possibly the balancewheel might have been near a magnet. On applying a needle to it, he found his suspicion true. The steel-work in the other parts of the watch had a perpetual influence on its motions, and the watch went as well as possible with a new wheel. If the soundest mind be magnetized by any prejudice it must, act þÿirregularly.

We ( IVexford Intlcpcmh at ) feel great pleasure in giving the following letter from a distinguished VVcxfordman, Commander M'Clure, of her Majesty's ship Investigator, addressed to his uncle, the Rev. Richard W. Elgee. Commander M'Clure was selected by the Admiralty to explore the Arctic regions in search of Sir John Franklin, and sailed t'rpm England on his mission in February, 1859. He has succeeded in discovering the North-west Passage, which has been sought after since the days of Alfred the Creat, but which important event in our history lias been reserved for one of Wexford's daring and chivalrous sons : " Her Majesty's Ship, Resolute, Doaly Island, " My dear þÿUncle. Burrow's Straits, April, 1S53. Your kind and most unexpected letter reached me through a travelling party dispatched by my excellent friend, Captain Kelle.tt, at a position on the opposite side ol these straits where we had been frozen in since 1851. The surprise caused by the appearance of strangers, where none were imagined to be within a couple of thou-

sand miles, was more than I can describe, and what can only faintly he imagined by any who have not been similarly situated, particularly when it was ascertained that two vessels and large supplies were so close at hand. The spirits of my crew seemed to revive, and from despondency to joy was hut the work ol' a þÿmoment the sick forgot their malajumping from their hammocks, were carried in the stream of human creatures up the solitary hatehway, which the severity of'the weather alio wed of being kept open, rushed on deckto he assured that the strange apparition was actually living flesh and blood, and not denizens of the nether world, for certainly their faces were black as Erebus, from cooking in their tents. When all was discovered to be real, and not a dream, my poor fellows, equally with myself, could not find words to express our thoughts ; the heart was too full, it was a call from the grave ; never, 1 trust, may the feelings of gratitude to the Almighty Disposer of events which then swelled in my bosom pass away. Many and great have been the mercies we have experienced in ourlong, tedious, and terrible navigation of that fearful polar sea, which has for four hundred years balded the navies of maritime Europe, and through which the directing linger alone of Providence lias safely guided us. All human agency was powerless, indeed, to advance us one yard m its accomplishment amidst the stupendous barriers of ice which never leaves its frozen surface. You will, I am cer-

' North West tain, be very happy to learn that the Passage' has been discovered by the Investigator, which event was decided on the 26th October, 1850, by a sledge party over the ice, from the position the ship was frozen in þÿ hut as in all probability mv dispatch will he published, 1 do not think it necessary to trouble you with further details; sufiicicnt to say we have been most highly favoured, both as respects the health ol' all, having only lost one man who accidentally poisoned himself about a fortnight since, as well as in being able to extend our searcli in quest of Sir John Franklin over a very large extent of coast, which was not hitherto known, and found inhabited by a numerous tribe of Esquimaux, 'who had never ere our arrival seen the face of the white man, and were really the most simple, interesting people 1 ever þÿmet living entirely hv the chase, and having no weapons except those used for that object. The of fiercer passions of our nature appeared unknown þÿ man fresh from his Maker's hand, and they gave me a pleasing idea uncontaminated by intercourse with our boasted civilization. All those who traded with the Company we found the greatest reprobates. On the and 7th of this month I left the Investigator, arrived on hoard here on the 19th, and was received by Captain Kellett with such a welcome as none but a ge licrous Irish heart could give ; indeed, the kindness we have received from all amply repays the toil, difficulties, dangers, and privations which for three

years we have endured. If the countrv and Admiralty only view our services which those we portion with hut a small have met evince there of the interest will he little left to complain of. » Every exertion is now being made to follow up the traces of poor Sir John Franklin, and it nothing is met with by the numerous parties that are now traversing the shores of this inhospitable and inclement country, nought will ever he heard to throw a light upon his mysterious fate, and search will have arrived at its utmost limits. I know nothing ot leaving us. the Enterprise, and can only regret het «> » "

Catechism for Young Girls who wish to re married. þÿ On Tuesday last two Paris booksellers appeared before the Tribunal of Correctional Police of that city, to dispute the ownership of a singular morsel of literature, entitled Instructions to Grown Girls who wish to be Married. In the course of the proceedings some passages of the catechism were read, which caused great amuseþÿ ment. The following is a specimen: þÿ YVhat is the most needful of all things for grown girls ? Matrimony. At what age ought girls to marry? According as they are pretty. At what age ouglil the prettiest girls to marry ? At 16 oi 18 years. But if they are not pretty, at what age? Whenever they can get a lover; they must not lose an opportunity. When a girl has not a lover, what must, she do to get one? There arc many means. What are those means? First, she must have prudence and modesty , second, she must show herself industri ous and a good manager; third, must always be very neat in her dress ; and fourth, she must not dress above her station, for that will drive away lovers rather than attract them. When a girl has a lover to her taste, what must she do not to lose him? She must love him truly, speak to him kindly, he always in good humour before him, and not coquette too much with his rivals. YVlicn a girl is demanded in marriage, what ought she to say? She ought to appear very much surprised, and then to say that she was not aware that a person for whom she had so much respect had ever thought of her.

in accordance with the order of the Government the Tax Commission for St. Croix will assemble on the undermentioned days, to receive information in writing relating to the taxes for the present year.

3TT AVIS For the Country : at 11 o'clock, viz : Tuesday the 22nd November for the inhabitants in both Eastend Quarters, at the Stock Estate Sallys Fancy, belonging to Lawyer Arnesen. Wednesday the 23rd November for the inhabitants in Companys Quarter, at the estate Work and Rest, belonging to the State Treasury. Friday the 25th November for the inhabitants in Queens, Kings and Northside Quarter Letr. B, at the Courthouse at Kingshill. Saturday the 26th November for the inhabitants in Princes Quarter, at the estate GroVe Place, belonging to the deceased Major Plasketfs heirs. Tuesday the 29th November for the inhabitants in AVestend Quarter and Northside Quarter Letter A, at the Courthouse No. 53 and 54 in Queens Street in Frederiksted. For the Town of Fredcrikstcd, on the same day in Strand Street, and AVednesday the 30th November for the inhabitants in Kings, Queens, Princes, Hospitals, New and Fishers Streets, Queens and Kings Cross Streets, Market and Hill Streets, at the above mentioned Courthouse. Besides those elucidations, which are required for the calculation of taxes to the State Treasury as well as to the Land Treasury, and which every owner or lessee of houses in and out of town, or of estates, is bound to give to the commission, the Government considers it requisite at the same time to be informed of the number of laborers on the estates or of other persons residing there as also of the quantity of stock on the estates etc., for which purpose the blank schemes for the tax lists arc furnished

with columns to contain such information. Owners of estates are to specify in writing the exact number of acres in cane cultivation and prepared for cane cultivation, or in other cultivation and pasture, used being or not in cultivation, neither nor yielding any profit. As to the land that yields no protit, the owner is to produce a certificate on oath signed by himself and two burghers of the Quarter, and attested as to its c.or rectness by the captain of the Quarter - Owners of houses that have been unoccupied for six months and upwards claiming a reduction in the taxes, are to give satisfactory proof of the house having been vacant during the period stated. Persons neglecting to produce the information, and proof prescribed by the regulations in the above shape, time and place, must ascribe to their own neglect all losses resulting therefrom. Blanks for tax lists will be distributed some days previous to the meeting of the Tax Commission and are required to be accurately filled out by the concerned, and delivered to the commission on that day, which is fixed on for each street in the towns, and for each Quarter in the country. JAMAICA. We extract the subjoined editorial paragraph from the Falmouth (Journal) 44 Trelaway," ' It is said that straws thrown of the 17th þÿultimo: up indicate the way in which the wind blows, and from one or two slight acts ot the new Governor, favorable auguries may be drawn as to the spirit which is likely to mark his future administration. The introduction of.inimigrants on a largo scale turned the fortunes both of Mauritius and British Guiana. Previous to the appointment of Mr. Higginson and Sir Henry Barkly to those colonies" were in a state of depression similar to that they into

3 If <e Ui <D 1 & ATI which Jamaica has sunk. They arc now in a comparatively flourishing condition, and the principal cause assigned for this change by Earl Grey, in his Pamphlet on the Colonies, was the importation of considerable quantities of Coolie, Chinese, and Portuguese strangers þÿ thereby enabling the planters to secure a steady supply of effective labor. Sir Ilenry Barkly rightly conjectures that what lias proved so advantageous for other colonics similarly circumstanced to our own, will be equally profitable in Jamaica. And with characteristic alacrity and promptitude, he seized the opportunity of a casual and unexpected call at Madeira, to engage some 300 Portuguese in families from the Agricultural districts, for the use of this Island. This is a God-send which will no doubt be thankfully received by those for whose especial benefit they were intended, but the manner in which the boon has been conferred deserves equal consideration. It is the procedure of one who evidently understands the im portance of seizing time value of the maxim, " bis dat qui cito datN It by the forelock, and the is as if he had said, the affairs of the colony are in a critical state, and the remedies required ought to be promptly administered. No time is to be lost þÿ and accordingly, the opportunity, as soon as it presented itself, was embraced. We infer from this, that the various other manifest wants and difficulties under which this Island labors, will meet with the same watchful care and energetic action þÿ and that as soon as the wheels

of the State machine arc fairly set in motion, our ecclesiastical judicial, and financial (as well as our agricultural) affairs will receive his immediate þÿconsideration, and no delay will take place in adopting measures for restoring the Island to a sound basis of prosperity." We are likewise indebted to the " Trelaway, of the 20th, for the following Speech of His Excellency Sir Henry Barkey, to the Legislature of Jamaica : " Mr. Speaker, Gentlemen of the Council , and Gentlemen of the House of " I have Assembly. called you together for a new Session, at the earliest opportunity of my arrival, earnestly thorised hoping that communications which I am au- by Her Majesty's Government to lay before you, may lead to the immediate termination of those lamentable , disscntions which have for nearly six months past deprived the Island of the fostering care of Legislature ; disorganised its public aud parochial Institutions, and materially aggravated its financial embarrassments, by suspending the collection of the ordinary Revenues. 4 ' It is far from my intention to advert in detail to the origin of the long pending disputes which have brought this to so unhappy a pass, still less to pronounce any opinion þÿ in the necessarily imperfect state of my knowledge upon the comparative merits of the position taken upon either side. 44 1 can perfectly sympathise on the one hand with the natural anxiety of the Representatives of a suffering community to reduce the cost of es-

tablishments generally into nearer proportion with its diminished wealth. I can on the other appreciate the reluctance of those whose constitutional function it is, to interpose a check upon popular impulse, to concur in arrangements which appeared to them uncalled for by the extent of the actual emergency, and at variance with those principles of good faith to which the State is bound to adhere as rigidly in dealing with its humblest servant as luau towards man in the transactions of private life. 44 But there is not so far as I can judge any thing irrcconcileable in these conflicting views, and I confidently trust that with the aid of a loan not exceeding £f)0,000, which the Mother Country is ready to offer for the purpose, you will be able in friendly concert, to devise measures, which, without pressing with greater severity than the circumstances of the time demand upon those whose offices it may on a general revision be determined either to abolish altogether, or to reduce' in value, will nevertheless ensure a large immediate diminution of taxation, than the most sanguine economist could heretofore reekou on. 44 It is my gratifying duty, however, to announce to you that I am empowored to hold out prospects of far more extendod relief to the productive industry of Jamaica than could arise from any possible reduction of official salaries ; in the shape of a guarantee by the Imperial Parliament of the entire Island debt, not already so secured. The benefit of such a guarantee would not be
confined to a mere temporary alleviation of the enormous annual burden which that debt entails since the reduction of the charge for interest would be so large as to enable you out of a portion of

the saving to provide for the gradual liquidation of the principal at no very remote period Nor would Her Majesty's Ministers, I am confident, hesitate to propose to Parliament, provided only the mode of regulating the revenue and expenditure of Jamaica be assimilated to that which has so long maintained the financial credit of Great Britain at the highest pitch to advance further loans to an extent sufficient for the introduction of a continuous stream of Immigrants to supply the void in the labor market created by the sad ravages of Cholera and Small Pox, and to aid in developing the vast natural resources of this beautiful Island more rapidly and effectually than its present limited population permits 41 The details of pecuniary operations of such magnitude will of course, require deliberate consideration, and 1 shall he ready at the proper time to communicate to you what further information I possess of the views of the government as to the securities aforesaid. 41 Meanwhile, I may briefly state, that the generous pnqiosals to which I have alluded, sanctioned as they have been with surprising unamity by the leading Statesmen in both Houses of Parliament, are founded upon no design of fettering in the slightest degree, that Legislative Independence, which for nearly two centuries, the people of Jamaica have so proudly cherished, are coupled with no conditions derogatory to the freest Representative constitution that ever yet existed, hut emanate solely from the sincere sympathy felt by the British Na-

tion at large for the misfortunes of (one of its most ancient and important Colonies. 4- It is in a similar spirit that you are urged by all parties at home, no longer to delay the introduction of such Political Reforms as the experience of the Mother Country lias demonstrated to he most conducive to efficient and economical Government, and best calculated to avert the recurrence of ruinous struggles between the various powers of the State. I well know with liovv much jealousy, suggestions of this sort must naturally he received by the large class, who, looking back to the efforts which it cost the earlier Colonists to erect the great bulwarks of civil and religious liberty in this Land, have learnt to regard the peculiar Institutions which spring subsequently thereout, as the acme of human wisdom. 44 Such feelings are worthy ot every respect, hut I must in all courtesy, remind those who entertain them, that no form of Government was ever yet so perfect as not lo require in the lapse of ages to he modified in accordance with the varying interest and progressive requirements of Society! Witness the British Constitution itself, the great mo del for the Colonial dependencies of tin Empire, which lias undergone so manysuccessive reformations for these ends, within a comparatively recent period ! 44 Here, on the contrary, a social revolution unparalleled in extent and com pletcncss in the annals of history, lias taken place during the last quarter of a century, with scarce any deviation from

the previous routine of public business þÿ What Jamaica stands pre-eminently in need of, at the present stage of hci political progress, is a strong Executive Administration, consisting of upright and intelligent men chosen from among bet own citizens, to devote themselves to the exclusive study of her condition, charg ed with the sole responsibility in all matters of finance þÿ and serving as an acknowledged medium of comntunica tion between the Representative of the Crown, the Council, and the House ol Assembly. In this way the harmonious co-operation of the several branches ot the Legislature., would be secured on every question of importance, and the theory of Representative Government he carried to its only legitimate conclu

sion. The improvements effected under such a system, in a governor's position would be, that the whole course of his policy could be disclosed to, and freely canvassed by the Colonist ; that there would be as little risk of collision between himself and either House, as between the Sovereign and Parliament, and that the time wasted in discussing bills to which it is wholly out of his power to assent, would be saved, and in many cases the irritating use of the veto avoided. " The bearing of the proposed change upon the relations between the Council and Assembly would be no less advantageous especially as there could no longer be the slightest objection on the part of the Crown to render the former in every respect as completely independent in theory as it has long virtually been in practice, or to add to it a large number oflanded Proprietors so as to identify it as closely as possible with the views of those permanently interested in the Colony. But the most beneficial result of all would be the opportunities afforded for the gradual introduction of well considered and wholesome reforms into every department of the Public Service, and for legislation of a more comprehensive and vigorous character than any individual member can be expected to originate and carry by his unassisted and unremunerated exertions. " I have dwelt perhaps, longer than I need have done on the first simple step towards the cure of the political disorders to which Jamaica is so peculiarly

subject, especially as I may have to address you again by message in referrence to the particulars of the plan. That plan may not prove a panacea for all the ills that afflict the colony, but at any rate it is no untested Theory of Government, no new fangled experiment in constitution-making, that is proposed as tjie basis of the guarantee to be given by tiie Mother Country for your debt ; but a consistent following out of the principles of the British Constitution through the introduction of provisions which can alone render the workingofthe Representative system in any country harmonious and effective. " Mr. Speaker , and Gentlemen of the Assembly. " It only remains that I should request you in her Majesty's name, to grant the supplies requisite, to meet the outstanding obligations of the Treasury, and to uphold the Public Establishments during the ensuing year upon an adequate scale. It is unnecessary for me to tell you of the ruinous amount of the claims, which from the lapsing of the usual Revenue Acts, are daily accumulating against the Island Treasury, or of the misery and distress thereby inflicted on all classes of the community. " Nor need I remind you of the even greater evils which must result from the expiration of the Rum duties, and from the parish Vestries being left without authority to raise funds for the support of the poor, or the repair of roads. " I feel satisfied that your regard for the public good will induce you at the earliest moment, to put a stop to evils

of such overwhelming magnitude. " I fear however that your wisdom may be tasked to the utmost to find the means of restoring the revenue to its former productiveness, owing to the large stocks of imported goods, which must affect the yielding of the Customs duties for a long time after their re-im position, whilst the excise on Rum can hardly for years be expected to recover. " This is the more to be regretted, because there can be no question of the desirableness of reducing at as early a period as possible, the very heavy rates imposed by the late Tariffs upon the

s tr. © 16, <© 1 3£ A T 'J 3 chief necessaries of life, þÿ as well as of abolishing as you have already had in contemplation, excessive charges as heretofore levied upon shipping frequenting " I earnestly your ports. trust that yonr local knowledge and experience may enable you to discover some method of providing for the expenditure indispensably requisite, without postponing such reductions indefinitely þÿ and I can assure you, for my own part, in perfect sincerity and truth, that not only shall I always be disposed to concur in every arrangement consistent with justice and efficiency, for lightening the public burdens, but that it is my anxious desire to secure the adoption of that systematic and searching economy which the depressed circumstancesofthc Colony imperatively demand. " Gentlemen of the Council. " Mr. Speaker , and Gentlemen of thi Assembly. " Gloomy as is the actual position of affairs, I see nothing to justify despondency in the minds of those to whom the future destinies of Jamaica are at this moment intrusted. " Much undoubtedly there is to afford ground for grave reflection and to enjoin extreme caution and forbearance on the part of all of us. " May II k, by whom the whole World is governed and preserved, inspire our deliberations with prudence and concord, and bless our humble endeavours to promote civilization and industry, and to restore happiness and prosperity to this distracted Country." þÿ From the Grenada Weekly Record , 'Movent bcr :i, 1853.

Antigua. A LOCAL GOV ERNMENT BANK While the prosperous condition of the settlement of British Guiana, and the Islands of Barbados and Trinidad afford cause for gratulation, unfortunate Antigua languishes, and her material interests are surely depressed. Painful as it is to us to make this statement, we shall, nevertheless, endeavour to account for the unhappy comparison, and to state that which appears to us to be, in some measure the cause of our misfotunc. The Island too, enjoyed, with those we have named, a large amount of prosperity previously to the passing of the Sugar duties Act in 1846. Up to that period, our staple productions yielded the proprietor a profitable return ; the Labourer was liberally rewarded for his toil ; and the Merchant and Tradesman wero satisfid with their gains. The effect of the Act soon, however, destroyed the general prosperity, and inflicted distress and privation upon every interest in the Colony. Sugar now barely realises the cost of its production, and the laboureris, in consequence, deprived of the amount of wages he formerly enjoyed ; while Proprietors, Merchants, and Tradesmen (in very many instances,) no longer maintain their credit. Unfler circumstances such as we have related, we deem it incumbent upon all whose interests are identified with the fate of the Island, to suggest or devise measures which may in any degree restore the. Colony to its former prosperity, or at least, alleviate the general distress To us it appears that

want of Capital for Agricultural purposes, is the principal cause of the existing depression, and this must naturally be the case with every Country whose prosperity depends solely upon the productions of its soil. The system pursued by the Colonial Bank in this Island, does not meet the requirements of a large proportion of the proprietors of Estates, and of other property, and it is therefore the duty of the Legislature to devise and adopt measures which shall enable the former, vigorously t«> carry on and extend cultivation, and the latter, l<> render available the benefits and advantages which property confers upon its possessor in very country except Antigua. The establishment of a local Government correspondent, " Mereator," in our last i.Auc, is Bank, suggested by our judicious and respected so much in accordance with our own views of the vast advantage which would be derived from|such

an Establishment, that we heartily, and at once respond to the suggestion, and pledge ourselves to the exercise of our best endeavours, (although at all times humble) to promote so important a desideratum And we hope that every patriot will afford his willing support and co-operation towards its attainment. A Bank, whose operations shall be regulated according to the mode proposed would relieve proprietors and other cultivators, from the necessity of contracting obligations which impose the necessity to ship their produce to certain markets, although better prices may be obtainable in the Island, or elsewhere ; enable them to extend their cultivation, and thereby afford continuous and increased employment to our peasantry þÿ an increase in whose number would, in such case, be most advantageous to the Island. The exports would necessarily be increased, and, the mass of the people being the contributors to the Revenue, the public income would be augmented, and the prosperity of the Merchant, the Trader, and Retailer, enhanced. Many other advantages, of which we shall treat on another occasion, would accrue to the Colony at large, and even to proprietors who may not avail themselves of its credit, by the establishment of a local Bank. The amount which would be required for the establishment of the Bank in question would be about £500,000, a sum which, we think, may readily be obtained. We are led to this conclusion, from the language of the Earl of Derby, in the House of Lords, on the tubjcct of a Loan to

Ireland for promoting Agriculture ; and the fact, that the Island of Jamaica has recently been liberally assisted with pecuniary aid from the Mother Country. Antigua having fulfilled her engagement by the repayment of the instalments and interest, upon the Earthquake Loan, it is reasonable to expect, that upon its being shown that a Loan of £50,000, (to be invested in a Bank for the purposes we have stated,) would be advantageous to every interest in the Colony, the amount would be obtained without difficulty. And to this object, we think the Legislature should direct its immediate attention. þÿ Observer , October 7.

RIl.TI FDEY FOR CHOLERA. The following letter was sent to one of our Ministers, and by his lordship at once forwarded to the Board of Health : þÿ My Lord, þÿ As I am in possession of a simple but effectual preventative to the spread of cholera, as well as a remedy of very great power for those attacked with the disease, I venture to apply to your lordship to have them made known, should it appear by trial that they are as effective as I have found them. As a clergyman, I have had many opportunities of trying the remedy, and in no case did the patient die, the recovery being always speedy and perfect. I make no apology for venturing to address your lordship, as the great importance of the snbject will be, I trust, deemed sufficient. The preventative is simply a small teaspoonful of powdered charcoal, taken three or four times a-week in a cup of coffee, or other vehicle, in the morning. When attacked with cholera a mixture of an ounce of charcoal, an ounce of laudanum, and an ounce of brandy or other spirit, well shaken together, may be given ; a teaspoon fnl every five minutes. In half an hour T have known this effectually relieve ami stay the disease As the patient becomes better the mixture may be given at longer intervals. I have known a patient in the blue stage, and collapsed, perfectly recover in a few hours. The charcoal was tried as a preventative on a large plantation in the Mauritius, and not a sin g!c individual out of 800 was attacked with cholera . Should your lordship think it well to make this

simple remedy known, it may save the lives of thousands, now that this dreaded diseases has visited our land. I have the honor to be, your lordship's very obedient and faithful servant, Charles Caulfiei.d. Creagh Rectory, Shibbereen. þÿ London Puprt i Thf. ST. Christiansted , Friday the 2?>th November 1 853 W k know, that all our readers will deeply and truly join in the expression of heartfelt condolence, with which we record in our pages this cruel bereavement, which it has pleased Him, who giveth and who taketh, to inflict upon our universally respected and beloved Governor. OBITUARY. Died on Tuesday last, Lady Jon anne J f.nsine Ingbrorg Catiirine Feddersen, born Deegen, Consort of His Excellency II. D. F. Feddersen, Commander of Dannebrog and Governor of these Islands, aged 37 years. The announcement of Lady Feddersen's death, has caused sorrow to many a heart that knew and prized her worth ; but it is a lesson softened and elevated by the reflection, that her pure spirit now moves freely and joyfully in the bright atmosphere of heaven. Accounts received from Constantinople of the I 10th state that the Sultan had made a formal de-' inand to the Ambassadors of England and France to summon the allied fleets to the Bosphorus. The Ambassadors had accordingly done so. It is said in a despatch from Bucharest of the 5th, that ated, " the camps had been broken up, and Rus- Prince GortschakoflPs inspection being terminsian troops were moviug in masses on the Danube, to the number of 35,000 men, with 251 guns." The Sultan's manifesto against Russia was read in all the mosques iu the capital on the 7th. It was not expected that the hostilities would commence before the 25th inst. The son of llcdschid Pacha, who has left Constantinople for Schumala, has, besides the summons to Prince Gortschakoff, despatches instructing timer Pacha what steps to take in case the Russians refuse to evacuate the Principalities. Prince Gortschakoff returned the following reply to the summons of Omer Pacha to evacuate the Dauubiau Principalities : þÿ My master is not at war with Turkey, but. T have orders not to leave the Principalities until the Porto shall have given to the Emperor the

moral satisfaction he demands When tbia point has been obtained, I will evacuate the Principalities immediately, whatever tin time or the reason. If I am attacked by the Turkish army, I will contine myself to the defensive It is believed that hostilities will commence in Asia, on account of the lateness of the season, and the theatre of war will probably be in the direction of Batoum, on the south-eastern shore of the Black sea. Volunteers abound iu Constantinople, but only Albanians are employed. Napoleon on the Future ol ICusiit and England. The following remarkable observa- St. Helena, are from O'Meara's " Voice tions of Napoleon Bonaparte, while at from St. Helena," vol. 2, from pages 69 to 72 and the surmises will he read with some interest at the present juncture : þÿ " In the course of a few years, Russia will have Constantinople, the greatest part of Turkey, and all Greece. This I hold to be as certain as if it had already taken place. Almost all the cajoling which Alexander practised towards me was to gain my consent to effect this object. I would not consent, foreseeing that the equilibrium of Europe would be destroyed. In the natural course of things, in a few years Turkey must fall to Russia. The greatest fiart of her population are Greeks, who, you may say, are Russians. The powers it would injure, and who would oppose it, are England, France, Prussia, and Austria. Now, as to Austria, it will be very easy for Russia to engage her assistance by giving her Servia and other provinces bordering upon the Austrian dominions, reaching near to Constantinople. The only hypothesis that France and England may ever be allied with sincerity will be in order to prevent this. But even this alliance will not avail. France, England, and Prussia united cannot prevent it. Russia and Austria can at any time effect it. Once mistress of Constantinople, Russia gets all the commerce of the Mediterranean, becomes a great naval power, and God knows what may happen. She quarrels with you, marches

off to India an army of 70,000 good soldiers, which to Russia is nothing and 100,000 canaille, Cossacks and others, and England loses India. Above all other powers, Russia is the most to be feared, especially by you. Her soldiers are braver than the Austrians, and she has means of raising as many as she pleases. In bravery, the French to and English soldiers are the only ones be compared to them. All this I foresaw. I see into futurity further than others, and 1 wanted to establish a barrier against those barbarians by re-establishing the kingdom of Poland, and as putting Poniatowski at the head of it king, but you imbeciles of ministers would not consent. A hundred years hence I shall be praised, (encense,) and Europe, especially England, will lament that I did not succeed. When they see the finest countries in Europe overrun, and a prov to those northern barbarians, they will " say Napoleon was right.'

The Daupliin again. The Fond du Lac Union, of the 28th lilt., says: The Rev. Eleazcr Williams, who has of late become famous throughout the United States as the supposed Dauphin of France, was in this city on Saturday and Sunday last. He preached two sermons at the Episcopal Church on Sunday. In a conversation we had with him on board the steamboat, a few days previous to his arrival here, on the subject of his parentage, he stated that evidence were being prepared for the press which would set the question at rest. Among other things, that the affidavit of his reputed mother, lately published, was a gross deception, not by her, but by the interpreter, (bribed, no doubt,) who falsely interpreted her language, This woman does not understand the English language, and when the substance of the published affidavit was afterwards told her, she denied ever having made it, and asserted to the contrary that she had made affidavit that he was not her son. Her statement will be contained in the forthcoming volume of evi-

8 SF A ? 1£ 8 dence, soon to be published by the reverend gentleman's friends. He expects to reap no advantage from the establishment of his identity as the heir to the throne of France, but regards the whole matter as merely a historical question, and as such it is an important one, to France at least. It is stated that there are those now living, in France, whose knowledge on this subject will be very important in the decision of the question, and among whom is the widow of Robespierre. Should the anticipations of the reverend gentleman's friends be realized, there may an important question arise with reference to the confiscated property of Louis XVI. þÿ Cincinnati Daily Times. Those of our readers who are unacquainted will find a full statement of them in " Putnams with the Pretensions of the Rev. E. Williams, Magazine for February 1853." þÿ En.

Strength of Insects. Should any of our readers be sceptical upon this point, perhaps the following illustrations of superherculcan strength with which the commonest insects are endowed, selected from curious sources, may prepare us to credit more easily the facts which we shall have to record in subsequent pages. The common flea, as every one knbws, will without much apparent effort jump two hundred times its own length ; and several grasshoppers and locusts are said to be able to perform leaps quite as wonderful. In the case of the insect they scarcely excite our notice ; but if a man were coolly to take a standing leap of three hundred and eighty odd yards, which would be an equivalent exertion of muscular power, perhaps our admirers of athletic sports might he rather startled at such a performance. Again: for a man to run ten miles within the hour would be admitted 1o be a tolerably good display of pedestrianism ; but what are we to say to the Delisle, " so minute as almost to be in- little fly observed by Mr. visible," which ran nearly six inches in a second, and in that space was calculated to have made 1,680 steps? This, according to the calculation of Kirhy and Spence, is as if a man, whose steps measured only two feet, should run at the incredible rate of twenty miles in a minute. Equally surprising are the instances of insect strength given by Mr. Newport. The great stag-beetle, which tears off the bark from the roots and the branches of trees, has been known to

gnaw a hole, an inch in diameter, through the side of an iron canister in which it was confined, and on which the marks of its jaws were distinctly visible, as proved by Mr. Stephens, who exhibited the canister at one of the meetings of the Entomological Society. The common beetle can, without injury, support and even raise very great weights, and make its way beneath almost any amount of pressure. In order to put the strength of this insect-Atlas to tiie test, experiments have been made which prove that it is able to sustain and escape from beneath a load of from twenty to thirty ounces ; a prodigious burden, when it is remembered that the insect itself does not weigh as many grains: in fact, once more taking man as a standard of comparison, .it is as though a person of ordinary size should raise and get from under a weight of between forty and fifty tons. This amount of strength is not, however, confined to the short thick-limbed beetles. Mr. Newport once fastened a small carabus, þÿ one of the most active and elegantly formed of the beetle-tribe, þÿ weight only three grains and a half, by means of a silk thread, to a small piece of paper, upon which the weight was to be placed. At a distance

ol ten inches from its load the insect was able to drag after it, up an inclined plane of twenty-five degrees, very nearly eighty-five grains; but when placed on a plane of five degrees' inclination, it drew after it one hundred and twenty-five grains, exclusive of the friction to be overcome in moving its load: as though a man was to drag up a hill of similar inclination a wagon weighing two tons and a half, having first taken the wheels off. þÿ Rymer Jones.

EDUCATION. Excellent Remarks of Bishop Dounot of freemen aine of New Jersey on this Subject : " We utterrly repudiate, as unworthy, only, but of men, the narrow notion, that there is to be an education for the poor as such. Has God provided for the poor a coarser earth, a thinner air, a the glorious sun pour sky paler down his gol- ? Does not den flood as cheerfully upon the poor man s cottage as upon the rich man's dren as keen a sense of cottager's palace ( Have not the all the fresh- chilness, verdure, fragrance, melody, and beauty of luxuriant nature, as the pale sons of kings ? Or is it in the mind God has birth, so that stamped the poor man's child knows the imprint of a base with unborn certainty that his lot is to crawl, " It is not so. not to climb ? God lias not done it. Man cannot do it. Mind is immortal. Mind is imperial. It bears no mark of high or low þÿ rich or poor. It heeds no bound of time or place, of rank or circumstance. It asks but freedom. It requires but light. It is heaven-born and it aspires to heaven. Weakness does not enfeeble it. Poverty cannot repress it. Difficulties do but stimulate its vigour. And the poor tallow chandler's son. that sits up all night to read the book which an apprentice lends him, lest his master s eye should miss it in the morning, shall stand and treat with kings, shall bind the lightning with an hempen cord, and bring it harmless from file skies. The common school is common, not as inferior, not as the school for poor

men's children, but as the light and air is common. It ought to be the best school, and in all good works a beginning is one half. Who does not know the value to a community of a plentiful supply of the pure element of water? And infinitely more than this is the common school, for it is the fountain at which the mind drinks, and it is refreshed and strengthened for its career of usefulness and glory." þÿ Universal Phonograpker.

We have long since felt the necessity of laying a plain statement of facts before our readers, by which they will be put in a condition to judge of the present state of our establishment. Not that we hereby mean to convince them of anything which we may here state, for that we believe to be beyond the province of Logic, but simply, to silence, if possible, their many objections ; and to lead them to consider, that perhaps, sooner than they expect, they may be deprived of the luxury of a Press þÿ the luxury wo say, for although in enlightened countries, a Press is looked upon as one of the necessaries of life, and supported as such, here, it is considered as a luxury and as such can be dispensed with. To begin therefore. þÿ In order to obtain the privilege of publishing a paper, we were obliged to agree to execute all Government and Public

yearly loss as follows : Work gratis. Burgher Council, Police and Sheriff Of- Government work This burden we estimate, at a ...... $600 fices, School Commissions, -c. . 300 12 Papers delivered to Government and other offices, a $6 yearly . 72

$972 which amount is also graced with an addition of a yearly tax of $16, which falls to the Polytechnic Institute in Denmark. Let it be borne in mind, that we have sustained this loss during the space of 29 years. Now a few facts will enable our readers to judge of our vast Revenues, which we are perfectly confident will not excite the envy of the most envious. 1st, We have a Subscription List of 56 Subscribers, amounting to $336 per annum ; of which one sixth pay their accounts ; the rest are perfectly content to pay us in small instalments, as convenient. Of course, we dare not discontinue their papers, for then they would only borrow their neighbour's and leave us the worse off. 2nd, Our job work is limited to perhaps a few hundred -Madeira and Old Port Labels in a year ; and latterly some Government Blanks, which, however, like Angels visits, are few " and far between." While here, we must also make a few observations on the subject. We arc often told, that we charge too much for þÿjob-work that 500 copies can be obtained in America at the cost of 100 here This silly observation but shews the ignorance of the nature of our work, on the part of persons who make use of it. We ourselves would be able to furnish 500 copies at perhaps but a trifle more than Jwe charge for 100 copies. The reason why this kind of work appears to be done cheaper in America is this : no respectable printer there would strike off 100 copies, unless he were paid as much as he would deliver 500 for ; consequently he al-

ways gets a large number to print. Of this we have a late example. We were offered the printing of 200 copies of a work for $300, which we very wisely refused. This work was then sent to America, where it was left optional to the author, to have either 600, 1000, or 1,500 copies for $2,000. No one here ever thinks of having more " than such a small number can't cost much 100 copies printed at a time, because but when their love of encouraging native energy prompts them to have their work have thousands done " while they are about done in America, then they find it best to it." Even Government blanks, and blanks for other offices, which have all been done in Europe or America, (until very lately, that we have received the former) were ordered by the thousands, and consequently obtained at a cheaper rate than we could furnish fifty or a hundred for. 3rd, As to our advertisements.' þÿ These are confined principally to such as the law compels to have inserted, and a few other unavoidable ones. As for the rest, every respectable merchant, with a niggardliness, worthy of petty shop-keepers and fruit sellers, prefers to post his written advertisements under the public galleries, than to have them inserted, because they would cost something. Now we refer our readers to any American newspaper. Let them examine the list of charges for advertisements, and see whether their charges are much less than ours. No one, we trust, can expect that we, with our high expenses for types <f-c. should

execute work at a cheaper rate than American printers. We would, in conclusion, ask our readers, if the above statement looks as if we are so "passing rich," when after paying our workmen, cost of paper with et cceteras, barely left with " forty pounds a year." like the poor curate we are Under these circumstances, we fear not candidly to state, that, should we not succeed in our endeavours to obtain from Government remunerato relinquish the publication of the " Avis." tion for their work, we shall absolutely be obliged We are as other men þÿ we cannot live on air, and therefore we repeat that unless our hurdeiiN are lightened we shall relinquish the undertaking. Perhaps some one else may be obtained, who will bo willing to groan and starve under the combined influences of gratis work, no advertisements, and bad-paying subscribers ; but for ourselves we þÿanswer NEVER

Objections to the correctness of the Lists, substantiated by proper vouchers and proofs, as well as the claims from such persons, who in conformity with 4 of the above mentioned Law deem themselves entitled to the Com pen sat ion- Money in preference to the original owner, shall be made by the parties concerned or some person duly authorized in their behalf, before the expiration of the aforesaid six weeks to the Judge of the respective Jurisdiction. The "AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 2nd December 1853. We are called upon to give publicity to the following remarks, which were made on last Sunday in St. John's Church, on the demise of Lady Feddersen.
Basin, Si. Croix, 2 ?th Nov. 1853.

The Rev'd F. J. Hawley, Rector of St. John's Church, Rev'd. and Dear Sir, We the undersigned members of your Vestry, deeming the remarks which you made in your sermon last sabbath, in allusion to the late lamentable death of Mrs. Feddersen, to be so appropriate to the poignant occasion which called them forth, and at same time so fully in unison with general feeling, that we are induced to ask from you a copy of the sermon for publication, so far as relates to this melancholy event, being convinced that your kind compliance in this respect will be gratifying to public sympathy, as offering, in some measure, a suitable tribute to the worth of one, who will long live in the affectionate remembrance of this community. We remain, Rev'd. and dear sir, Yours most respectfully, JAMES BROWN. Wm. II. WOODS. ADAM Mc'CUTCIIIN. CHARLES LUCAS.

i Concluding remarks of the Rector of St. John's Church on Sunday last. In tlic mysterious Providence of God, I am called to a more painful duty, the notice of a most mournful and afflictive dispensation, one that in our short-sightedness we are utterly unable to fathom. That the most excellent Consort of our highly esteemed and universally beloved Governor; the accomplished Lady, the warm hearted and prudent friend, the most affectionate

wife and devoted mother, the impartial hostess and iriend of the poor ; should have escaped the pestilence of the last year, to be suddenly called away at this time of comparative health and prosperity, is certainly a dark and mysterious provi- Gods " way is in the sea, thy path in the great dence, that confounds all human wisdom. Surely waters, and thy footsteps are not known." So sudden and awful a blow, inflicting so irreparable a loss, has seldom if ever been struck in this community. W'c feel that society has lost its brightest ornament, and virtue aud religion their highest and most effective support ; and wo are almost struck dumb in the presence of such a calamity. We feel the inadequacy of language to express our sorrow, and that submissive silence is perhaps the most fitting and eloquent tribute we can render. The Psalmist's become us : " 1 was dumb, I opened not my deportment under a sharp affliction seems best to mouth, because thou didst it." To say that Lady Feddeksen was peculiarly fitted for the high station she adorned and tilled with so much grace and wisdom ; that she had won the esteem aud affectionate regards of this whole community ; that they who knew her best, appreciate her most ; that she was the pride of a fond husband ; the kind mistress ; and the most exemplary and affectionate mother ; all this seems trite and cold and common place, when we reflect upon her pure and unexceptionable life from the first moment of her arrival among us to the sad hour of her

death in the past week. This sorrowful and mourning community witness to the greatness of the loss which society and religion have sustained. Aud well may we mourn, Brethren, when we consider the fearful responsibility which attaches to rank and station, and how little it has sometimes been regarded ; when one reflects on the readiness of a community to take shelter in the example of an acknowledged superior. It is when we reflect upon the genial and happy influence of religiou aud virtue in high stations ; upon the thousands of immortals on every side ; that as christians we begin to realize the great loss this community has sustained. It really seems, my Brethren, as if we could see nothing but judgement for our Island in this afflictive stroke. It seems to call loudly upon every inhabitant of this land, to humble himself before the Lord aud to turn to llim in weeping, fasting, and in praying. But instead of dwelling on that con jugal affection aud simple piety ; that train of virtues which graced her character, and endeared her to us ; let us rather strive to see our own nearness to that world whither she has gone. Let us view this solemn visitation as dying men. Let us sec to it, lest returning prosperity and the all-absorbing cares of business are in danger of causing the claims of Christianity aud the interests of the church of God to be forgotten and despised ; and thus we have required some such solemn and mysterious Providence as this to recall our thought-

less hearts back again. It addresses us in this character, and speaks to us a language which affects not this community only but a world. I pray that the spirit of God may send homo its sacred lessons to every heart. May lie lodge this solemn truth in all its energy, within our souls : " Behold thou hast made my days as an handbreadth, and mine age is as nothing before thee ; verily every man at his best estate, is altogether vanity." And, dear Brethren, is the Bible the only teacher of this humiliating truth ? The events of every day, the observation and experience of almost every hour, speak the same language . With what a powerful voice is the solemn truth now sounded in our cars ? There has been a grave opened in our midst that sends it home to our very hearts-! It shows us the nothingness of man, by forcing us to remember the prccariousncss and little worth of all the earthly blessings we call our own. There is not, my Brethren, one of them that we can be sure of retaining even for an hour. Have we a beloved child or friend, our only hope and solace in a dreary world : Death, before we are aware, may strike a blow, which will rob us of them. Have we a wife endeared to us by innumerable offices of love ? She may be a corpse stroke as this call on us to Brethren, to-morrow. O how loudly, have no idols upon does such a earth, to set loose to the dearest earthly connection and to lean only on our God ! A husband or a wife, parents or children, are wretched subthem in the morning ; but " the wind stitutes for the rock of ages. Wc over them," and in the evening " they rejoice over arc gone." passeth

The same mournful scene shows us too the little use which earthly blessings arc to us, while we retain them. Who more blessed with'all the world can give, than she whose loss has filled our sland with weeping r And yet what could it all do for her in the hour of need ? Neither the

skill of physicians, the tears of a beloved husband, nor tin; prayers of an anxious people could keep off even for au hour the hand of death. How olten have wc been forced in the few years of human life : " Man dies and his expectations that are past, to observe the abrupt termination perish." The thread is snapped asunder almost before he has begun to wind it. The hand, often stretched out in deeds of mercy, is now motionless ; the head encircled by a shroud ; the generous heart, that once glowed with the thought of scattering blessings around us, is as cold as a stone ; all the fond associations connected with the name of mother, are buried in the grave. Let then the robust and the healthy, the wise and the learned, the rich and the great, learn here a lesson. No rank however elevated can lift us above the common mortality of man, nor any degree of poverty sink us below it. The beggary are alike preludes to the shroud : " All robes of the great and the tattered garments of flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass." 0 why then, Brethren, should we all be so fearfully careless about every thing which relates to the soul and eternity. This mournful occasion should forcibly remind us of the great duty of consideration. This carelessness is inherent in our nature, and no power but that of Hod can root it out. The God of mercy is acquainted with this bane of our nature, and in compassion to our souls he employs his providence to awake us out of this dreadful sleep. Has then this

mourntul dispensation which is so fresh in our memories produced this effect ? If it has filled our eyes with tears, and our hearts with grief, has it made us feel the precariousness of all our earthly blessings ? The vanity, the uncertainty, the shortness of our own lives ? The nearness of eternity to our own souls ? Are we prepared to die ? Is the great business of life begun ? Are we employing our time seriously in seeking the treasures of salvation ? Wo see, Brethren, that we must soon be in eternity ; what have we to hope for there ? What is " stored up for us in that everlasting home ? () cease from man whose breath is in his nostrils." O " put not your trust in Princes, or in the son of man in whom there is no help ; his breath goeth forth ; lie rctucneth to his earth, in that very day his thoughts perish. Happy is he who hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in his Lord God." Let us, dear Breath era, lie low as weak, guilty and helpless sinners, before the Saviour's cross. There may be found a life of happiness, a death of peace, aud an eternity of joy.

The following astonishing statement of a Steam-ship building in New York, we find in the Herald of the 1st October : þÿ " Tl»c i\ Day Steamer."

Mr. John W. Griffiths is progressing " the six day steamer" þÿ with the steam-ship William Norris, or such having been the time designated in which she will make the trip from this city to Europe. In her present unfinished state, (her frame being hut partially raised when seen by us,) it is of course impossible to say much of her model. Her ends will evidently he sharp, and from the flatness of the flooring already laid, she will doubtless he very buoyant. Her dimensions are þÿ length, 275 feet; beam, 37 feet ; depth, IB feet. It will be seen that her beam is very wide in proportion to her other dimensions þÿ at least seven feet more than that of ordinary vessels of her class þÿ which, with her light draft, it is anticipated will add materially to her buoyancy. The engine that is to carry the vessel in such an unheard of short time across the stormy Atlantic, will be equal, it is stated, to 1,200 horse power. The cylinder will he 72 inches in diameter, with a stroke of twelve feet, and capable of standing a daily working pressure of 45 lbs. The wheels will he 36 feet in diameter. In order to counteract any strain that might result from the use of so much power, she will have three iron kelsons, from eight to nine feet deep, extending the whole length, and strongly secured to the deck and bottom. The main features of the experiment are lightness of draft, sharp and buoyant model, and great power, combined with extraordinary strength þÿ and it is by this combination that the projectors calcu-

late to make the trip across the Atlantic, in fair or foul weather, within the short space of six days. It is stated that in proportion to her displacement, her power will he more than double that of vessels of her class, and that she will travel nearer the speed of her wheel than any vessel afloat, on account of her extreme lightness and perfection of model. We cordially wish them success. þÿ lhid.

From the St. Thomas Times, Jan. 7, 1853. Precautions against and Treatment of Cholera.
We copy the following valuable memoranda, relating to the prevention and treatment of Cholera þÿ which scourge unhappily reigns in our midst þÿ from

Q m <D sn A T a 3-« our contemporary of the St. Kitts " Gazette" ; and we doubt not that our readers will find them acceptable just now: 1. þÿ Prevention is to be carefully studied ; therefore all kinds of fiuit, salids, peas, cucumbers, celery, and pickles, bad better be avoided when Cholera is prevailing þÿ also oysters, lobsters, crabs, ntussels, Or other shell-fish; solid food is better than fluid, therefore it will be well to abstain from the use of soups, hashes, &e. 2. þÿ Wet and cold should as much as possible be guarded against by warm dry clothing and lodging. 3. þÿ Cleanliness, both of the person and the habitation, should be especially attended to, and the walls of houses should be well whitewashed, and all dust-bins, sinks, drains, water closets, and cess-pools, should be kept as clean as possible, and a portion of Chloride of Lime, or solution of Chloride of Zinc, sprinkled upon them daily ; ventilation is always necessary to the enjoyment of health, and when Cholera is prevalent the inhabitants should be cleared of all unnecessary lumber, and as much air as possible admitted, and caused to pass through them. Cholera is not contagious, so that no one need be afraid to attend upon any person who may unfortunately be attacked.

TREATMENT: Cholera is generally preceded by more or lessof bowels complaint, sometimes for several days previous, sometimes only a few hours. If a person is attacked with purging, put him or her immediately to bed, apply bottles of hot water to the feet and stomach, nnd let him be kept quite warm ; give him 20 drops of Laudanum, 10 drops of essence of Peppermint, in a wineglass of hot Brandy and Water, and continue to give the same dose (as long as the purging continues) every two hours; when the pain is relieved, and the purging stopped, you may next day give one or two tablespoonsful of Castor Oil to clear the bowels of any irritating substance, but should the looseness of the bowels continue, give 20 grains of the compound Chalk powder, and 10 drops of Laudanum, made into a draught, with Peppermint water after each loose motion. Barley water ts the best drink, and Rice well boiled, the best food until all purging has ceased. Cholera comes on with cold, giddiness, sickness, vomiting and purging of what looks like dirty water, or rice and water. If the Patient be cold and feel chilly, let him be put into a hot bed, cover well with blankets, apply bottles of hot water, or bags filled with hot sand or hot brand to the stomach, along the back bone, and feet; put a large mustard poultice made with vinegar, over the stomach, and keep it up for 20 minutes ; give 15 drops of the " Anti-Cholera Drop every ten minutes, in a wineglass of brandy and water. If perspiration comes on give hot tea to drink,

with a teaspoonful of Brandy in each cupful. If cramps come on, the Legs should be diligently rubbed by the hands of two or three persons at the same time if possible. The patient should be allowed to drink as much as possible of milk and water, toast and water, or simple cold water. After Cholera subsides, a Fever sometimes comes on, which lasts several days, in this disease it has been recommended to give 5 grains of Quinine every night, and 2 grains morning, noon, and afternoon. The diet

should consist of Eggs, Milk and Rice, or similar food, Meat appears to be injurious for a long time, in any form, even as a broth. When Diarrhoea prevails, without any Cholera having manifested itself, the first thing is to clear the Bowels completely by the following dose : Castor Oil, one ounce, tincture of Rhubarb, half an ounce, compound spirits Ammonia, thirty drops, Peppermint water, one ounce, made into a draught, and half an hour afterwards take a basinful of thin Gruel, with a tablespoonful of Urandv in it. If the looseness of the bowels continues, give 5 or 10 grains of Mercury with Chalk, at bedtime for two or three nights, and 20 grains of the compound chalk powder in a draught of Peppermint water three limes a day. As 1 have reason to believe that the ' Anti- Cholera drops" will be found very serviceable, not onlv in cases of Cholera, but in all spasmodic affections of the stomach and bowels. I annex the formula for the preparation, take essence of Peppermint, 2 ounces. (1 part oil to 8 parts spirit) compound spirit of Ammonia, 1 ounce, Laudanum, 6 drams, tincture of Camphor, 6 þÿdrams mix.

The United States frigate Columbia, 50 guns, and a crew of 485 men, Commander Penoergrast, bearing -the Flag of Commodore Newton, arrived here on Sunday last, in 14 days from New Yoik. As she entered the harbor His Majesty's Sloop-of-war Saga, lying at anchor, hoisted the American Flag at the fore, and gallantly saluted, which was soon after replied to bv the frigate, which displayed the Danish flag at the fore. Later the frigate saluted Fort Christian and was answered. It being found that the>e were two cases of Small Pox on board, the authorities here desired that the frigate should proceed to the quarantine ground and hoist the green flag, which was immediately complied with. On Wednesday the patients were removed to the l.azeretto at Munenfeldts Battery, and the frigate released from quarantine. On Thursday forenoon Commodore Newton landed, and was received at the wharf by a guard of honor from Fort Christian. The Commodore proceeded to Government House, where, we are informed, be has taken up his temporary quarters þÿ Ibid, December 24.

On Wednesday the U. S. war-Steamer Fulton, 6 guns, Captain Vatson, in six days from Norfolk, arrived here. This may be considered a very quick run. It is reported that other portions of the American home squadron are expected here, and will rendetvous during the winter months þÿ Ibid.

A HIGHWAYMAN. In the autumn of 1817, a complaint was made at Hatton-Gardcn police office by two ladies, who staled (hat they had been robbed in the following singular manner; while walking near battle-bridge about six o'clock in the evening, a dog, unaccompanied by any person, sprung suddenly from the road side, and seizing hold of the reticule which one of the ladies had in her hand, forcibly snatched it from her, and turning off the road, made his escape. A constable stated, that a dog answering the same description had also robbed a poor woman of a bundle containing two shirts, some handkerchiefs, &e., with which he got clear off. Several other instances of a similar naiure were mentioned, and the general conclusion was that the animal had been trained up to the business, and that his master was in waiting at no great distance to receive the fruits of this canine plunderer.
