Oil the Danube there has been a tacit suspension of operations, which is attributed to the severity of the season. Omar Pasha has abandoned all his positions on the left bank of the river, and cantoned his troops in winter quarters on the right bank, after completely destroying the batteries at Oltenitza. He has left, however, on the island of Turtukai, two regular battalions and a battery, to hold possession of this spot. The General-in-Chief occupies Kalafat, on tlie left hank of the Danube, the fortifications of which he has strengthened, and the garrison of which he has greatly increased. In the retrenched camp, close to the town, there are 40,000 regular troops of all arms under the command of Ismail Pasha of Circassia.

TO MELANCHOLY Farewell, vain mirth, and noisy joy#, Ye gay desires þÿ alluring toys ; Thou, pensive melancholy, deign, To hide me in your silent train.
For oft by night I musing rove, Where artless shades embrown the grove, And oft, where winds in caverns groan, I wander silent, and alone.
Come lovely mourner, sweetly sad, In sorrows garb, in sable clad, Henceforth, dull carc my thoughts employ ; And sorrow be my only joy.
By tombs, where gloomy spirits stalk, Familiar with the dead I walk ; While to my sighs and groans, by turns, From graves, the midnight echo mourns
0 Happiness ! vain empty name ! Say, art thou bought by gold, or fame ; Ah ! what is gold, but shining earth ? The common fame, but common breath ?
Come, thou sweet friend of virtuous woe, With awful pace, demure and slow, For sad and pensive I'll pursue, Thy steps þÿ adieu, vaiu world, adieu

It was on the 20th of last, month the news reached us, that Cholera had broken out in St. Thomas. In consequence of which the Government with a precision that is worthy of notice, immediately called together the Board of Health 5 and the sanitary precautions, which experience has elsewhere shewn to be effectual in checking the ravages of this dreadful epidemic, were at once adopted. The Board of Health issued instructions with regard to the treatment and prevention of Cholera ; and 800 copies were printed for distribution gratuitously. Several members of the community were called upon to inspect thedifferentyardsj and tosec that, all rubbish and filth be removed. The requisite Quarantine Regulations were

3T» AT33, revived 5 the public bridges and walls were ail white- washed ; and the gutters properly cleaned. These measures are considered public ones 5 and if they had been neglected, the Authorities would have been censured severely, for not d ing what is right and necessary. They have, how#ter, been punctually attended to ; ant! we must now turn to private individuals and ask them, it there is nothing wanting on their part ? Have they done, or do they intend to do, their duties as good and upright citiz ns? We fear not 5 for already we have instances of their mammon speculation and avaricious desire to extort from the public an unfair profit on their articles. ( 'holera, it is true, is very near u's; but should this circumstance war- as rant such unjustifiable speculation we see now practised ? Surely not. Merchants and Shopkeepers, who have bad the entire or greater part of their stock of Provisions 011 band before Cholera appeared in St. Thomas, and consequently free of any additional cost to them, demand now an unreasonable profit. Book at the size of bread ! Look at the price of Provisions þÿ Candles, Pork, Butter, Lard, Cheese, Biscuits, Soap, &c. People are obliged to pay exactly double now to what tbev bad to pay before. Such measures as these call loudly for reform ! !

GREAT FIRE AT NEW YORK. We learn that there had been an extensive conflagration in New York on the 10th December, which broke out in the large publishing and bookselling establishment of Messrs. Harper and Brothers in Franklin Square. The fire commenced at No. 2 3 & 26 Pearl Street. The entire establishment of Messrs. Harper and Brothers was one mass of rubbish ; comprising six houses on Clifl Street, running through to Pearl Street, and taking in the same number of houses in that street. The loss is stated at three quarters of a million of dollars. The loss of the Harpers is fixed at $350,000; they are insured for $25,000 in various Insurance Companies in the city. This is the second time the Harpers have been burnt to the ground.

The Illustrated London News, Dec. 31 . It is generally believed in Paris that the Emperor of the French has insisted upon a positive determination on the English Government in accord with France ; and that after some hesitation, the Earl of Aberdeen had subscribed to all the conditions of the French Government in the contemplation of vigorous action against Russia. It was added that Lord Palmerston had consented to resume office under these circumstances; and that he was coming to Paris to have a conference with the Emperor. It has been currently reported in Paris during the past week, that the English and French Governments have now very little hope of a pacific solution of the Eastern question, and that France and England are about to make preparations for an expedition to the Baltic early in the Spring. Sir Charles Napier is to command the English fleet in that sea. The orders given to the French and English squadrons are said to be to cruise in the Black Sea in such a way as to constitute a sort of impassable maritime harrier from Varna to Bataum, not permitting either Turkish or Russian fleets to cross the line hut leaving each of them perfect freedom of action on their own side. This would be a less offensive act than the blockade of Sebastopol.

A few years since, a wealthy gentleman of Paris, who lived in idleness, at length became weary of life, and left his house one evening, with the intention of drowning himself in the river Seine; it being yet twilight when he arrived at its banks, he concluded to walk about a short time, till it was datker, so that he should not be discovered. While thus engaged he put his hand in his pocket, and felt a purse, which was filled with gold; he concluded to go and find some poor family, and give it to them, as it would do no one any good, if tie cast himself into the river with the money. He soon found a poor dwelling that bespoke poverty within ; he entered it, and there he beheld the mother of the family stretched on a bed of sickness, and some six children in rags, and crying for bread. He gave them his purse of gold, and immediately their tears of sorrow were transformed into tears of joy; and their gratitude was so ardent and simple to their benefactor, as to fill his heart with joy and peace, and he exclaimed, " 1 did not tiefore know that there was so much happiness in doing good. 1 abandon the idea of killing myself, and will devote the remnant of my life to doing good." He did so, and was much distinguished for his deeds of benevolence. þÿ Universal Fhonographer.

A SPILL LIFE þÿPICTURE NANKIN. Nankin is situated on an immense plain, intersected by canals, as numerous as those which traverse the human body. In the nudst of the fertile fields, innumerable rivulets and streams of navigable water are perpetually crossing each other. The hanks are planted with willows and bamboos, with strait stalk and dark foliage It is on the plains of the province of Nankin that that yellowish cotton is grown, which, when woven, is exported in such enormous quantities. Here also is reaped the greater part of the rice which is consumed throughout the Empire. The Kiang-Nan, or province of Nankin, is the richest jewel in the crown of the Son of Heaven " " Nothing in Europe can give an idea of the fruitfulness of this province þÿ neither the plains of Beauce nor the plains Lnmbardy, of nor even the richest of lands, Flanders. In the Kiang-Nan the fields are covered with crops twice a year, and produce fiuit and vegetables without cessation. On the borders of the arable land, the most delicious vegetables in the world are produced. The pre-tari, a cabbage, which is between a let-

tuce and a cabus, bitter mustard, water melons, potatoes, and the hundred species of harecots produced in the Celestial Empire. We have been fortunate enough to sit under the shadow of the orchards which border the On-Soung, one of the numerous veins which fertilise the Provinces of Kiang-Nan; we have plucked with our own hands those pulpy jujubes which travellers often taken for grapes; pomegranates with transparent grains; monstrous peaches, by the side of which the finest kinds of Montreuil would appear like wild fruit, and diospyros as large as tomatos. We have seen scarlet pheasants, and their brethren with mother-of-pearl plumage running freely about the furrows. This province maintains 28,000.000 inhabitants, ten times as many as Holland, and rather more than the whole of France. Nevertheless, our worthy countrymen who fancy that our nation is the most rich and powerful, also imagine that their country is the most populous in the universe. Nankin is built in the water. It is a city like Rotterdam, surrounded by fertile marshes, atid waters abounding in fish. Towards the south the river suddenly widens, and forms a kind of lake scattered over with innumerable islets Here, under clumps of trees, are hidden the villas of the mandarins. In these mysterious retreats they conceal from the envious glances of the vulgar their aviaries stocked with pale birds, reared in the cases of Seu- Tcheon-Ton, that city of delights which a Chinese proverb says, " In the other world there is a paradise; in this there

is Sou-Tcheon-Tou." These poetical women, these Aspasias of the East, compose charming verses in their own naif and impassioned language ; but the jealousy of their masters only allows them to sing their compositions on these echoless banks. On the indolent waters of the lake, as well as on the more rapid waters of the river, sail the most elegant vessels in the world. Thousands of junks bear to the extremities of the Empire all the produce and manufactures of the country. Nankin is the residence of the literati, the men of science, the dancers, the painters, the antiquaries, the jugglers, the physicians, the poets of celebrity. In this charming city are held schools of science, arts, and pleasure; for here pleasure itself is at once an art and a science; Malte Brun asserts that in this learned city there are even an lnslitu'e and an Academy of Medicine. None but a Geographer could spread such a calumny; at Nankin there is neither an academy nor academicians. þÿ Translated from French.

THE TURCO-RUSS1AN WAR. | THE NAVAL MASSACRE AT SINOPE FRENCH ACCOUNT J Although several accounts of the affair at Sinope have been published, the following French account will be read with interest ' The Turkish fleet, composed of seven frigates, three corvettes, and two steamers, left the Bosphorus to cruise in the Black Sea, but was soon after separated in a heavy gale. The Pasha who commanded the squadron put into Sinope, where he was soon after joined by some of his vessels. He afterwards sent his steamers in search ot the missing ones, and the whole were eventually united at Sinope. They were anchored without order, and badly placed for an attack, when, on the 27th of November, two Russian ships of the line and a Brig came into the bay, and. passing within gunshot of the Turks, proceed- I ed to cruise near Cape Tuich. The Russian brig, there is no doubt, then went to give information to the main body of the Russian fleet, either at sea or in the harbour of Sebastopol. of the position and strength of the Turkish squadron. The latter, expecting that an attack was to be made, changed its position, but without placing the vessels in uch a manner as to be properly covered by the batteries on shore. About noon on the 30th the Russian squadron, composed of six sail of the line, three of which wore threedeckers, two sailing frigates, and three steamers, entered the bay, the frigates and steamers remaining outside the heavy ships. The line of battle ships anchored near the Turkish vessels, and immediately lowered and armed

their boats. About half-past one o'clock in the afternoon, at the moment when a boat was pushed off from the Russian Admiral's ship, the frigate of the Turkish Admiral opened her fire. The Russian vessel recalled her boat, and immediately the action commenced. All agree in saying that the Tutkish vessels and the Egplian frigate fought with the greatest bravery, but, over-powered by the superior weight of metal of the Russian vessels- they were soon silenced. After an action of half an hour one frigate blew up, an hour after two others met the same fate, and in about two hours and-a-half all the squadron had either blown up or were on shore. One corvette alone remained at an-

© m © a a atis. chor, but in a crippled stale, and the Russians endeavoured to tow her off as a prize, but, finding that she was making water very fast, they set fire to her, ar.d she was soon destroyed. At the commencement of the action a Turkish steamer, which was anchored in shore of the Turkish squadron, got under weigh on a signal from the Turkish Admiral, and endeavoured, by running along shore, to gain the offing. The frigates and, for a short time, one of the line of battle ships made sail i there. That monument of cold-blooded and after her, and fired broadsides at her, but she effected her escape, and is the only vessel which escaped from the disaster of the day, and it is this vessel which brought the news to Constantinople. At the moment of the action there were in the roadstead an English merchant vessel, an Ottoman transport, and six small Turkish merchantmen. All these have either been burnt or sunk. Two of the English crew were drowned, and the remainder embarked on board the Retribution frigate. with the exception of the master, who proceeded to Trehizond with the agent of Lloyd's. During the action two small batteries on shore fiied on the Russian squadron, but the others could not fire, as the Turkish vessels lay between them and the enemy's ships. When the firing had ceased the Russians manned their boats and boarded the vessels which had run on shore, in order to make prisoners of any one of the crews they might find. The Tuikish admiral, several captains and officers, and a certain number

of seamen were taken. The vessels to which the Tuiks had not set fire when they were abandoned were burnt by the Russians. There only remained on shore two vessels, a 24-gun corvette and a brig, which have not been burnt. All the part of the town between the arsenal, wftere a frigate was on the stock, and the citadel has been burnt. Soon after the action a fourth Russian steamer joined the squadron in the roadstead, where the ships were occupied in repairing their damage. The loss sustained by the Russian squadron is not known ; their rigging appeared to be much cut up The Turks seem to have generally fired too high; the wind blowing in shore, all the smoke drove towards them, and they fired at hazird without being able to see their enemy The wrecks of the vessels on shore were still burning when the account left. The coast was covered with wreck, and dead bodies are constantly being washed on shore, where they are buried by the inhabitants. It would appear that the firing of the Russians could not have been very good for them to have taken so much time in destroying the Turkish squadron A surgeon who was on board one of the frigates that blew up affirms that his vessel fought for two hours before she took fire, and at that moment she had lost 200 men, killed, having been exposed to the fire ot two Russian line of battle ships. From the small number of wounded which were found in the town, and from the nature of the wounds, which appear to have been mostly caused bv the explosion, it is supposed that almost all

the wounded were burnt with the vessels It is impossible, in the confusion of such a disaster, to ascertain how many were able to escape on shore. The total number of the crews on board must have been about 4,000, half of whom, at least, have been destroyed. The only importance attached to Sinope is in its port and its position ; it has no longer any commercial interest attached to it It has a

quantity of excellent building timber on the coast, but it can never recover from its ruin without the powerful assistance of Constantinople." The scene of war and desolation that presented itself on the arrival of the steamers from Constantinople was horrible indeed. Nothing in the warfare of the most barbarous period, and on a similar scale, could surpass in cowardlv ferocity what has taken place

wanton vengeance will never be effaced from the memory of Europe. The massacre, continued even after all resistance had long ceased, shows a savageness of nature which feels no generosity for the conquered brave nor pi t v for the helpless and unoffending. When the Retribution and Mogador arrived on the spot they found every house destioyed, or still in flimes, and the town almost utterly uninhabited, mangled bodies and limbs floating about or rotting upon the beach, and the dead or dying scattered among the still burning fragments that strewed sea and shore. It is a fact that, even after the docks and ships were destroyed, the Russians pouied an incessant shower ol grape and canister on the poor wounded wretches who weie snuggling amid the waves and striving to teach the shore, as if the thirst foi massaoie could not be stayed while one human being survived. The massacre and confl igration, llie treacherous ferocity of the assailants, ami the desperate heroism of the victims were absolutely awful. The effect produced at Constantinople by the sad feelings was terrible. Crowds of people collected in the streets and accompanied the families of the victims of Sinope to the residence of the Capudan Fasha. on whom the fault is laid of having sent to the Black Sea a squadron so weak and so unprotected, when it was known that the Russians were prowling along the eoast of Asia Minor. From the London Morning Herald, December 31, 1853. From the period when Russia began to mingle in the politics of Europe, now more than a century and a half ago, the course of that power has been marked by fraud, by treachery, by falseness, and planned by double-leading. Her schemes are In and artfully worked out. generally long them there is uniformly exhibited a rare union of congruity and cunning, mingled with a certain boldness, dash, and bravado, likely to dazzle and captivate the minds of a semi-Asiatic and wholly superstitious and barbarous people. Peter the Great knew his countrymen well, and it is to this union of the daring and the mysterious, by which he alternately dazzled and deceived the savages subject to his sway, that his successors have recourse, nearly 130 years after his death, to deceive and dazzle the Russians of 1854. A genuine Russian Mujik believes that nothing is impossible to the Czar. He places his Emperor on a level with his God, and in the ordinary exclamation so frequent in the mouth of a Russian peasant, God and the Czar are great," you find " the measure alike of his wonder and his worship. It is the special business of functionaries and officials to exaggerate this blasphemous manworship, and to make the army and the navy, as well as the peasants and serfs (which are convertible terms in Russia), believe that nothing is impossible to a descendant of Peter I As Peter I. led armies north and south, and bribed and intrigued where he could neither intimidate or conquer, so do his successors servilely follow in

his path. Peter I. had designs on Sweden, ou Denmark, on Mecklenburgh, on Ilolstein, on Constantinople, and on Persia, and so have those successors, who have succeeded to his ambition and fanaticism without succeeding to any portion of his genius, daring or fortitude. Peter the Great, from his naval education, aspired to make his flag float in every sea, and, sooner or later, to render himself master of the Sound, the Belt, and the Kattegat ; and his successors are only following his injunctions, if not his example, in sending ships to the Pacific, and fitting out frigates to sail to Japan and those islands between the 31st and 48th degrees North latitude. But though it is our bounden duty to keep our weather eye fixed on the proceedings ot the Russians in the far-off sea of Okhotzk and the waters of Japan, yet for the present, and indeed for the whole of the year 1854, we may safely leave the Muscovite ships in these waters to the superintending care of Brother Jonathan, who is represented by Commodore Perry, of the United States navy We may be quite sure that the pupils of Mentsohikoff and Nachikoff, if they ever turn up at all in the latitude of Nipon, will be kept to their very good behaviour by the ship or ships of our cousins on the other side of the Atlantic. The intrigues of Russia in Sweden and Denmark must, however, be met in a very different manner. At both those courts the representatives of England should hold a bold and a manly language þÿ a language which would find a respon-

sive echo in the hearts of the Swedish and Danish people. It is the greatest mistake in the world to suppose, as the Abcrbeen organ supposes, that the present Monarch of Sweden, Joseph Francis Oscar, who has now been nearly ten years on the throne, has any predilection for the Russian Court or system of government. Though, on the whole, the reign of that remarkable and able man, his father, was favourable to the prosperity and happiness of his adopted country, yet it cannot bo denied that the latter years of the reign of Charles John XIV. (Bernadotte) were far from being popular, and this was altogether owing to the belief, wrongly or rightly entertained by his people, that he generally exhibited too decided a leaning to the politics of Russia Strangers are

sf» ®m®as£ A T 'i 3. by no means popular in Sweden, either as settlers or rulers. But, despite this prejudice, Berna- dotte got over the reproach of being " un Go seen qui avait gagne a lotcric sans y mettre," though he never got over the somewhat merited imputation of including the Russian dynasty and system. It there be one feeling more strongly and more ineradicably intertwined with the very existenee of a Swede than another it is inextinguishable hatred of the system and policy of Russia. Bernadotte, doubtless, thought that in rendering himself the tool and accomplice of Russia he was securing a fast friend and ally ; but he little thought how this mistaken policy alienated from him the affections and respect of the people over whom he was called to reign. Fortunately for himself and for his dynasty Bernadotte died in 1S44, for, had he continued another year or two in the course of his unpopular subserviency to Russia, it is very questionable whether he might not have been forcibly exported in 1845 to the country from which he had b:en originally imported in 1809. The present King of Sweden has formed a policy diametrically opposed to that of his father, and therefore much more in harmony with the wishes of his people. Arriving in Sweden at nine or ten years of age his wishes and feelings are identical with those of the country, and this is one of the causes of his popularity. Ilis first declaration on assuming the reins of power was to the effect that he would not follow in the footsteps of his father þÿ that is to say, that he would

not be the mere instrument and tool of Russia. The reform of the criminal code and other internal reforms are due to the present Sovereign ; and in his external policy he had the good sense to take a course diametrically opposed to the policy of his father. It cannot be too prominently stated, that it was in the reign of the present Monarch, when the Northern Monarchs had violated the treaty of Vienna by the extinction of Cracow, that Sweden protested on this infraction of public law in manly and energetic terms. This, no doubt, was a most significant act, more particularly at the epoch at which it was performed, and it is not to be for a moment supposed that a Monarch capable of taking so enlightened and just a view of his own duties, and the rights of other nations, should in anywise sanction the spoliating and pirating proceedings of the great disturber of Europe, and the hereditary enemy of the Swedish, Norwegian, Finnish, and Scandinavian races. The absence of Sir Edmund Lyons from his post at Stockholm might be, at such a moment as the present, regretted, if the character of Oscar were not so raised above suspicion of any complicity with the Czar, or if Sir Edmund himself wero not rendering excellent þÿ should we not say better þÿ service in the Black Sea. The people of Den-

The humble Petition of the Council and Assembly of the Island of Grenada, Siieweth : þÿ That your petitioners have received with deep regret the sudden and unexpected announcement of the intention of your Majesty's Government immediately to withdraw all your Majesty's troops from this Colony, and to abandon the military works and fortifications, thereby leaving to the inhabitants the new and heavy burthen and expence of self-protection. That in the year 1783 and in the subsequent years from 1785 to 1792, this Colony furnished largely and liberally both labour and money (as will be seen from the annexed statements and Act of the Legislature) towards the construction of those works and fortifications, and the purchase of the land on which they are erected, on the assurance and pledge from the then Minister of the Crown, that a Military force of two regiments of the line should bo stationed here during the time of war, and not less than one regiment of the line in time of peace. That your petitioners humbly conceive, that, from the statements furnished in the annexed documents, the case of this Colony should form an exception to that of the other Colonies. That, impoverished and reduced as this Colony now is, from measures of imperial legislation, which they could neither control nor avert, any new burthen imposed, at this time, upon their already exhausted means, must necessarily be attended with accumulated distress. That your petitioners therefore humbly pray, that your Majesty would be graciously pleased,

for the relief of this Colony to permit one company of your Majesty's troops to remain stationed in this Colony for the protection of the persona and property of your Majesty's loyal and devoted subjects therein. And your petitioners, <J'C Weekly Record, Grenada Dec. 29.

From the Observer, January 1, 1854. C n I N A. THE INSURRECTION Woosung. þÿ Constant fighting is going on, with little result on either side. The losses of the Imperialists have been considerable, while the insurgents have suffered little, which gives them confidence. The imperialists have received large reinforcements, and were estimated, of all kinds, at about 14,000, and the foreign vessels hitherto employed at Chin-kiang-foo have come down to assist. The fleet of junks which passed through on the 13th ofSeptember, ordered by the Taoutae, was seen close to Woosung, and, unless the insurgents receive assistance from Nankin, it is doubtful if they will be able to hold the city for any length of time against such a force. VARNA IN THE BLACK SEA. Varna is built on one side of a deep bay on a large plain, extending to the foot nearly of the Little Balkan. The town is surrounded by a high wall and broad ditch, not very deep. The fortifications are now in perfect order, and many new outw orks are skilfully thrown out. built substantially of large sods and fascines. Heavy guns are mounted on the outworks. There are about 210 guns mounted altogether nearly all 68 þÿ þÿ none less than 48 þÿ about 60 face to sea. There are six gates; three are now kept shut, and all are shut up at halfpast four each evening. On the opposite side of the hay from Varna is a high ridge, in which heavy guns are mounted, and strong fortifications erected. A signal staff also is there. This ridge completely commands milcsand not more than two Varna, for the hay is a half across. The holding ground is first-rate, and with an outlay of a few thousand pounds a most perfect harbour might be made, by building a breakwater. The bay is exposed to south-east winds. On Hie Conclusion of the Year Consider first, that the year is now come to & conclusion ; it is just upon the point of expiring; all these twelve months, that are now past, have flowed away into the gulf of eternity ; they are now no more : they shall return to us no more. All our years pass in this manner, they all hasten away one after another and hurry us along with them, till they bring us also into an endless and unchangeable eternity. Our years will all be soon over : we shall find ourselves at the end of our lives, much sooner than we imagine. 0 let us not then set our hearts upon any of these transitory things ! let us despise all that pass away, with this short life, and learn to adhere to God alone, who, never passes away, and be prepared for our departure hence. Consider 2ndly, that the year is as now past and gone, so arc all the pleasures of it : all our diversions, all our amusements, in which we have spent our time this year, nre now no more : the remembrance of them is hut like that of a dream. 0 such is the condition of all things that pass with time ! Why are we not practically and feelingly convinced of the emptiness and vanity of them all : and that nothing deserves our love or attention but God and eternity ? And as the pleasures of the year arc all past, so are all the displeasures and uneasiness, pains and mortifications of it : they are also now no more than like a dream : and so will all temporal evils appear to us, a little while hence ; when we shall see ourselves upon the brink of eternity. Let us learn

then only to fear those evils which will have no end ; and the evil of sin, which leads to these never ending evils. Consider 3rdly, how you have spent your time this year. It was all given you by your Creator, in order to bring you forward to him, and to a happy eternity. 0 how many favors and blessings have you received from him every day of the year ! How many graces and invitations to good ! And what use have you mado of theso favours ? What virtuo havo you acquired this year ? What vico have you rooted out ? What passions havo you overcome Havo you made any improvement at all in virtue, sinco the beginning of the year ? Instead of going forward to God, havo you not rather gone backward ? Alas ! what an account

3 'i\ $ 1U S :£ A T Jt 3 shall you have to give one day for all this precious time ! and for all these graces and blessings spiritual or corporal, which you have so ungratefully abused, and perverted during the course of the year ? Then as to your sins, whether of ommission or commission against God, your neighbours, or yourselves : which you have been guilty of this year, either by thought, word, or deed : what a dreadful scene will open itself to your eyes, upon a little examination ! And little have you done during the course of this year, to cancel them by penance ! 0 how melancholy would your cause be, if your eternal lot were to be determined by your performances of this past year ! Conclude by giving thanks to God, for all his blessings of this year ; and especially for his patience and forbearance with you in your sins. Return now at least to him with your whole heart ; begging mercy and pardon for all the sins of your life. And resolve with God's grace, if he is pleased to give you another year, to spend it in such a manner as to secure to your souls the neverending year ofa happye ternity. þÿ Grenada Paper.

A Jonathan. þÿ Among the notions at the New York Exhibition we are told of "a new printing press, which prints from uncut paper, rolling from a cylinder, and cuts and folds with perfect regularity, thirty thousand copies per hour. There is counteraction in t he process, and consequently no time lost in returning motion. Both sides are printed at the same time, and thirty thousand per hour is a low estimate, since, hy increasing the speed, they can he printed as fast as paper or cloth can lie unrolled from a cylinder. The inventor declared that he can print one mile of news-paper as fast as a locomotive can run on a railway. With perfect machinery and arrangements he may do it. llis present experiments demonstrate a practical principle, and the invention is looked upon with wonder and delight." The only difficulty will he in finding editors to keep pace with the machine. þÿ Jamaica Paper.

Pen-and-ink Sktch of the Czar. þÿ The Emperor is of a great height, and is very proud of it ; too proud, perhaps, as he lias acquired the habit of certain airs, which often give him a strong resemblance to a peacock when about to spread his tail. It is a fact well known in St. Petersburg, that every well grown man newly recruited for the guard is carried into the Emperor's presence, who measures heights with him. His air is serious, his glance wild, even a little savage; his entire physiognomy has something hard and stern in it ; his gestures are abrupt, and he cuts his words in pronouncing them. The Emperor never shows himself hut in the military costume, the stiffness of which is in perfect keeping with his tastes, and which makes his great height still more conspicuous. Meanwhile there is a want ofease in his movements ; since a fall from his horse, he drags one leg after him, in a disagreeably inelegant manner. þÿ The Czar and the Sultan.

Turkish Husbands and Turkish Wives. þÿ They arc often uxorious, and, in case no suspicion of jealousy crosses their minds, treat their wives with considerable deference. Few will venture to appear in the presence of their ladies in the slightest degree intoxicated ; and they will submit to be beaten on the day of Eeriam, if fiom poverty, or other causes, they have been unable to bring home the roast shoulder of mutton required by inexorable custom for the family dinner of that day. Eastern ladies often resort to this sum- I mary mode of proceeding with their lords and

masters, even when not protected by the privilege of a festival. It is true that, on the other hand, they are exposed to similar treatment if they carry the joke too far, or misbehave in any way; and that the þÿsack of which it is now the custom to make fun among wags who have looked at the outside of eastern þÿmanners is always ready to punish serious deieliction of duty. Once married the Turkish women consider themselves free; and, indeed, they enjoy far more freedom than we are accustomed to believe in Europe. Their veils and hideous uniform costume keep them in a state of permanent disguise, and with this advantage, under pretext of paying visits to friends and relations, they may go where they will in company with their slaves. Only the wives of the Sultan and some great viziers are now encumbered with the unpleasant attendance of eunuchs A not uncommon place of resort is one of the public cemeteries, where hasty intrigues are often formed with soldiers, peasants, the first comer, in fact ; for it is perfectly absurd to expect to find our notions of morality, save as wonderful exceptions, in a country where all the conditions necessary to their growth are wanting.

Detection by an Emetic. þÿ An eccentric doctor having missed a quantity of currants, inquired of his housekeeper what had become of them. She said she could not tell htm, never having seen them. The doctor ap. peared satisfied, but in a short time his housekeeper looked ill, and asked to feel her pulse. After doing so he pronounced her very ill, and prepared a draught for her, which she took accordingly, and to her great consternation presently the missing currants began to make their appearance, the draught being an emetic purposely administered by the doctor.

From Me Observer, January 1, 1854. THE EASTERN QUESTION AS IT STANDS. The Constantinople letters confirm the inelligence that the ambassadors of France ind England had not sent the fleets into the Black Sea, but had demanded instructions from their respective Cabinets ; that the protocol and note of Vienna had arrived; that Reschid Pasha had received them favourably ; and that a grand council was to be held to take them into consideration. There was a talk of removing the Seraskier Pasha from his place because he was too much disposed for war, and of nominating Riza Pasha to succeed him, Reschid Pasha, becoming Grand Vizier, and Aali Pasha Minister of Foreign Affairs. Amongst the rumours current was one of a complete change of Ministry, with the view of bringing in men more favourable to peace. The Sultan and all the population were painfully affected at the disaster of Sinope ; it was generally believed that the Capitan Pasha (Minister of Marine) would be dismissed, as mainly responsible for it, he having, as alleged, given Osman Pasha orders to remain in the Bay of Sinope, though the French admiral several times pointed out to him the danger of his so doing A popular demonstration had been made against the Capitan Pasha. About 200 women, belonging to the district called Cassein Pasha, which is chiefly occupied by the families of sailors, had been to the Admiralty, had broken the windows, and had made such violent threats against the Minister that he had deemed it prudent to escape in disguise.

He had been warned that he would have to appear before the Council of Ministers to explain his conduct. In the event of his being dismissed, Ahmet Pacha Kaiseli was spoken of as his successor. The Ambassadors of England and France, supported by the Ministers of Austria and Prussia, were energetically pressing on negotiations for peace, and, it was confidently asserted, not without hope of success; but the Sultan, though entertaining a great horror of war, was afraid that any project of an arrangement would cause profound commotion in the empire þÿ the catastrophe ofSinope having caused immense irritation. Besides this, it was expected that the effect produced on the Western Powers by the disaster of Sinope might be such as to effect an entire change in the situation. Accounts from Asia had been received, in which it was stated that the Turks had gained advantages over the Russians ; that, for exampic, the Russians had been repulsed in a new sortie from the fortress of Alexandropol ; that the Turks who were besieging the citadel of Akiska had succeeded in destroying the aqueducts; that Selim Pasha had gained a brilliant victory in the environs of Saffah ; and that Daniel Bey had defeated the Russians in the Terek. The news that Persia had broken off with Turkey, and had resolved to second Russia, had created great sensation. She was assembling an army of 50,000 men to march on Bagdad. She owed 60,000,000 piastres to Russia, but the latter had agreed to abandon the debt. The Turkish Ambassa-

dor at Teheran had at rived at Bagdad, on his return to Constantinople. The English Minister at the same place was also expected at Constantinople. On the other hand, Dost Mahomed, Sovereign of Afghanistan, who is an implacable enemy of Russia, strongly op-

3 3T A T H 3. posed the policy of Persia, and even threatened to invade her territory to avenge the Turks. General Baraguay d'Hilliers gave a second grand dinner on the 1 4th, to which he invited the admirals and most of the principal officers of the two fleets ; and Lord Stratford de Redcliffe gave a grand dinner on the 15th» to all the foreign Ministers, the admirals, and most of the Ministers of the Porte. The weather was very bad in the Black Sea. On the 13th the Belgian vessel Eugenia, Captain Hergeirch. was lost at the entrance of the Bosphorus. An English merchant ship from Trebisond had brought tiding that a Russian ship of the line, which had been lowed greatly damaged Irom Sinope, had gone down about 90 miles from that place. The Divan had given orders to fortify 16 important points on the coast of Anatolia, on the Black Sea l'he Porte has published a circular, ordering the Turkish authorities who may, during the delay accorded, have relations with Russian merchant vessels, shall observe a conciliatory conduct, and even render them services when opportunities occur. þÿ þÿ"OOOo UNCLE TOM'S CABIN. Let us imagine one of our critical successors of a century þÿhence that is, in the month of October 1953 þÿ sitting musingly before a copy of a work called Uncle Tom's Cabin, which a few days previously he had taken down by chance from one of the least-used shelves of his library. May one also amuse one's imagination by a picture of the possible state of things then existing on the other side

of the Atlantic, by the light of which our shadowy friend of 1953 has read the work which his substantial one of 1853 has just laid down ? þÿ The present United Slates of America, after having been, perhaps, more than once split asunder and soldered together again þÿ or the whole, or a large portion voluntarily reannexed to the mother country, and by and by again þÿdetached after these and other possibly more or less sudden, violent, and bloody vicissitudes þÿ have become a great Empire, under the stern, but salutaiy, onewilled sway of the Emperor of America: his majesty a jet black, who had shown consummate and unexpected high qualities for acquiring and retaining the fear and submission of millions of the stormiest tempers of mankind ; but his lovely empress a white. He has an immense army devoted to his person and will, composed of men of every complexþÿion from black, through copper-middle tints, down to white ; and correspondingly diversified are his banners, but black, of course, the predominant; a quadroon being commander-in-chief. As for his majesty's civil service, he has a coal-black chancellor, equally at home in the profoundest mysteries of white and black letter; a mulatto minister of instruction, and a white secretary of state ; black and white clergy and a similarly constituted þÿbar here a big black face frowning out of a white wig, and there a little white face, grinning out of a black wig, with black and white hands, and gowns varied ad libitum.

And the laws which they are concerned in administering, aecord with these harmonious þÿdiversities it being, for instance, enacted under heavy penalties, that no black shall, by gestures, speech, or otherwise, presume to ridicule a white because of his colour, nor, vice versa, shall a white affect to disparage a

black because of his complexion ; that the emperor and empress shall always be of different colours, and that the succession to the throne shall, alternate between black and white, or mulatto, be members of the imperial family. By this and other provisions have been secured a complete fusion between North and South, between black and while, glitteringly typified by intermingled gems in the imperial crown; the central one being the identical black diamond that figured in the famous Exhibition in Great Biitain in 1851, and presented to the emperor by one of the descendants of her Majesty Queen Victoria, then on the British throne I " To this complexion " shall it be that matters have <' come at last ?" Or will our sturdy cousins of 1953 be still republican, a united republic, but with offices, honours, rights and privileges, equally distributed, as in our financial empire, among those of every shade of colour ? Or, after a fearful taneous ry, after a . succession of struggles between black and white.. the From a preliminary dissertation prefixed . . . . .. sang þÿ is predominant ; . . slave- . . or a noble sponto the book, our critic of 1953 learns that it excited, almost immediately on its appearance, a prodigious sensation among all classes, both in Europe and America ; that both sexes, high and low, young and old, literate and illiterate, vulgar and refined, phlegmatic and excitable, shed tears over it, and wrote and talked about it everywhere; that, within a few months' time, impressions of it were

multiplied by millions, and in most languages of the civilised world. That its writer, an American woman, immediately came over to England, and made her appearance in public assemblies, called in honour of her ; and she was also » lionised" a word explained, in a long note, as indicating a custom prevalent in that day, among weak persons, of running after any notorious person weak enough to appear pleased with itj among the fashionables and philanthropists of the day, but preserved, nevertheless, amidst it all, true modesty of demeanour, and silence amidst extravagant eulogy. Inflamed with curiosity, our shadowy successor sits down to peruse a þÿwork then possibly little, if ever, mentioned þÿ anxious to see what could have produced such a marvellous effect, in the middle of the intelligent nineteenth century, on all classes of readers; and whether it produced permanent results, or passed away as a nine days' wonder. Having at length closed the pages of Uncle Tom's Cabin, and judged it according to the critical canons of 1953, will he deem it adequate to have produced such effects ? What estimate will he form of our intellectual calibre? þÿ Black Wood's Edinbugh Magazine.

From an official account of the 18th instant, received from St. Thomas, we learn that a violent Diarrhoea has broken out there on the Estate Hull, situated on the Northside of the Island ; and that 6 persons had fallen victims to it Every precaution was immediately taken to prevent any intercourse between this and other places ; but a single case of the same disease lias notwithstand-

a «ev» A 'T 3. ing proved fatal on the Estate Caretbay, situated | just by the side of the Estate Hull. Although we very much fear that this disease is the malignant or Asiatic Cholera, still this , supposition has not been confirmed by the King's Physician. On account of this information, and as Cholera is at present raging in the Island of Nevis, the Government has requested the Quarantaine and Sanitary Commissions in both jurisdictions, to take precautionary measures as well to prevent this scourge from being communicated from other places, as also to prevent it extending itself here. We would therefore recommend cleanliness in houses and yards, white-washing and ventilation of rooms, orderly diet, temperance, and no excess in dancing and carousing in the night.

THURSDAY, 17 NOVEMBER. The Court þÿ Mr. Francis said he would know this man if he saw him, hut lie had known Andrew before. The learned Counsel proceeded þÿ With such witnesses on the floor, it was for the J ury to deal with them. He rejoiced at the expression of the witness, that he would like to see them all hanged. As to Rrown, he does not know how long lie was in the passage, but he knows the prisoner was there ; he did not speak as to any particular circumstance. We have no evidence of the witness having spoken to him. The Court þÿ But the witness, Brown, states he heard him say he would make this a St. Domin- go- The learned Counsel continued , þÿ . Brown says ' he was in the alley. Now, Gennlemen, what I would impress on you is, may not some other man have been mistaken for the prisoner ? There is not a gentleman in that. Box but must know that the witness might have been mistaken. This, gentlemen is what I want you to arrive at ; he might have been mistaken. Mr. Bryan only seeing him from the window might have been mistaken. As to Sophia Amey, slje is a person who undertakes to swear to the faces of a whole mob. They might have been mistaken. All I wish to arrive at, gentlemen, is that there is a doubt as to the identity of this man ; and if you doubt, you will as eonscientious and honest men find a ver- dict of " Not Guilty." Mr. Isaacs spoke as the correctness of the witnesses' testimony, leaving no room for doubt. The Court as before stated the requisites to he

proved, and went through the evidence, shewing how the facts had been spoken to by the several witnesses ; and as regards Mr. Felix Francis' expression that he wished them all hanged, it amounted to this, that he wished to sec justice done, hut though such expression had better not have been uttered, this did not disqualify the witness. As regards his coming forward to give evidence without being subpocned, this was the duty of every honest man in the furtherance of justice. His Honor then showed with what certainty the prisoner had been identified by all the witnesses; and he could not agree with the learned Counsel that his presence was spoken of unconnected by any circumstances particularly drawing the attention of the witnesses to him. Mr. Felix Francis says his attention was particularly drawn to him in the first instance standing near to him, saying " God damn the by a man tjueen." Brown heard him say he would make this a second St. Domingo. Mr. Bryan knew him well ; he met him on the hill, when he threw a brick at him. And Sophia Amey says that she saw him throwing stones from the bill. Mr Bryan's testimony confirms hers as to the circum- | stance of his being on the hill. However, if after ' all the Gentlemen of the Jury had a doubt, and that doubt was a reasonable and conscientious doubt as to the identity of the prisoner, they would give the prisoner the benefit of it. The Jury returned a verdict of " Guilty." There are other Indictments against this prison-
er for offences committed during the riots, and subsequently to the firing of the Town. The prisoner was remanded to jail, to be brought up when the Court shall require him to receive sentence.

FRIDAY, 18th NOVEMBER. The next prisoner tried was Henry Harrigan , for setting fire to the house of Thomas S. Buntin and Henry 0. Buntin, on Tuesday, the 2nd of Augqst. When the person reporting these trials came into Court, the Jury were empanelled, and Jim Shew alias James Smith was under examination þÿ lie spoke of the house belonging to Mr. Thomas Buntin, called the Old Custom-House, and lately occupied by Mr. Justice Pringle. þÿ The prisoner said he was, going to burn Tommy Runtiu's right and title ; he had a brand of fire in his hand taken from the burning wood of Mr. Shew's house ; it was a piece of pitch pine blazing. The prisoner set fire to the house ; he opened the door under the gallery ; he went in ; another man broke some of the banisters and gave him ; he set fire in the Southern corner ; when lie came out 1 saw the fire blazing through the door. In reply to a question asked by one of the Rioters, he said he had done it well. I know the prisoner well; knew him when- 1 was droghing ; he has a lame hand ; he carried the fire in the lame hand. Cross-examined by prisoner's Counsel þÿ Were you drunk or sober that day ? I was sober; there was nothing to be got to drink. I was standing in the street when lie entered with the stick on fire ; I tried to save my things ; he carried in- the fire, and shut the door ; I said, for God's sake don't do it. He walked up Town, and I tried to save my things. The other one said, have you got it ; he said I have well got it, and the flames

rose up. I don't want the Jury to believe I saw through the door ; I saw him go in with the fire'; the other one broke the banisters and handed it to him. I saw him come out, and the other fellow asked him if he had got it ; he set fire in the S. E. corner ; that is the < orner the fire came out of. lie carried in the tire, and the trash and the wood. After he said I have well got it, I saw the fire blazing from the door ; I know him by name ; he took the fire from the house that had beeu burned þÿ Mr. Shew's house. He set fire to this house (meaning Mr. Buntin's house), and- this house caused other houses to burn. What caused him to set fire to Mr. Buntin's house r He gave me no explanation. Mr. Shew's house was burning " the innocent must suffer for the guilty." I saw ; the rafters had fallen in . He said him the whole day ; saw many others ; saw no one setting fire but these three men ; did not see Mr. Buntin that morning ; said it was what Mr. t it Buntin did, had Mr. Buntin been there he would have thrown him into the fire. Re-examined þÿ It was this man set the fire ; there is no other house I would describe as the Old Custom-House. Felix Francis sworn þÿ I know the prisoner ; can't mistake him ; saw him on the 2nd of Augt. whilst the stones were throwing ; saw liirn throw a stone ; saw the stone fall, it did not touch the house. 1 noticed that his right hand was affected ; I lived in Mr Buntin's house ; this house is called the old Custom-IIousc ; 1 was a tenant ; I left the house ; while I stood at the gate I saw

this man with a piece of burnt hoard in his hand, contending with some others which was Thomas Buntin's house ; whether it was the one I had left, or whether it was one of Mr. Crooke's. This man went under the gallery, opened the door, went into the end room with the fire ; the other man who was with him ordered him to set fire, and to do it well. While this man Was in the room, I saw the smoke coming out ; he came out and shut the door, and said, " let me sec the damn man who would open that door." I afterwards went round in the yard, recollecting that Sue lived there, and told her to come out of the I room, for the house was on fire. That was the house Mr. I'ringle had lately left ; it was nearly opposite Mr. Shew's house. Cross-examined þÿ The prisoner was enquiring which was Mr. Thomas Buntin's house. Mr. Henry 0. Buntin sworn þÿ I owned jointly with my brother two large houses in town. They are both burned. One was on a sea lot ; this was the house formerly occupied by Mr. Pringle, and recently as a Custom-House ; that house was burned. I did not sec the prisoner set fire ; after he was in prison he sent for mc ; he acknowledged that I had given him advise to go peaceably home on the 2nd of August ; he did not know it was my house, hut he was told which it was ; and he was given a stick of fire, and told to set. fire to it, which he did. Mr. R. M. Isaacs Q. C., summed up the evidence, and left the ease to the Jury.

Prisoner's Counsel þÿ The question arises in my inind whether or not the prisoner upon the Indictment might not be indicted for setting fire to Mr. Henry Buntin's house. The Court þÿ Unless the evidence has identified the particular house, the prisoner must be acquitted. The learned Counsel þÿ The prisoner has been indicted for setting tire to a house belonging to Messrs. Thomas and Henry O. Buntin, with intent to injure. You, Gentlemen of the Jury, must be satisfied that the intent to injure applied to Mr. Henry as well as to Mr. Thomas Buntin. The intent to injure j\Ir. Henry 0. Buntin has been negatived ; and the learned gentleman argued that from the evidence such a deduction might fairly be inferred, and that being the ease, ho must claim an acquittal of the prisoner. The Court summed up, reading over the whole of the evidehct', and the learned Judge stated that it was not necessary to prove the intention to injure all the parties suffering byr the act of the incendiary ; but in this case it had been shewn that the intention was to injure Mr. Thomas as well as Mr. Henry Buntin. The learned Counsel requested the Court to direct the acquittal of the prisoner, inasmuch as the Indictment stated the house was situated in the Parish of St. George, and no evidence had been given that the house was situated in that Parish. Mr. Isaacs, Q. C., said that was unnecessary, as by an Act of the Legislature the whole of the Virgin Islands were declared to be one Parish, and that the situation of the house had been des-

cribed with sufficient certainty. The Court would take a note of the objection. a verdict of " Guilty," and the prisoner was re- The Jury after retiring a few minutes, returned manded. The Court adjourned until to-morrow.

Mr. Huggius, Counsel for prisoner Henry llarragan , asked if the Court would hear argument touching the objection he took, and which the Court noted, namely, that the offence for which the prisoner was found guilty having been said in the Indictment to have been committed in a certain Parish, namely, the Parish of St. George, it was essential to establish the Indictment to prove that the house burnt by the prisoner was situated in the Parish of St. George, and that no evidence had been given to that effect. The learned gentleman admitted that the words " in the Parish of St. George,' might be superfluous, but those words having been in the Indictment, it was necessary for his learned friend to have proved them, and that it was no answer to the objection to say that the whole of the Virgin Islands were one Parish. The learned gentleman then read some authorities bearing on the point. Hon'ble. JL M. Isaacs, Q. C., contended 1st, tnat the ( ourt wen bound to take judicial notice of all public acts, and of local divisions of counties, þÿ -c. the whole of the Virgin Islands being but one Parish, the Parish of St. George, and the offmoe proved to have been committed in the Road Town of Tortola, it was sufficient. Next, the words "in the Parish of St. George" were superfluous, and he need not prove them ; it was sufficient to prove with certainty the situation of the house ; this had been done. law produced by the learned Counsels argument The Court retired to consider the þÿ and on the and

May it please Yont Homous þÿ We, the Grand Inquest of the Virgin Islands, beg to thank Your Honors for the very comprehensive Address delivered by His Honor the President of the Court at the opening of this unexampled Session. The perspicuous and forcible exposition of the I, aw applicable to the principal cases likelv to come before us in connection wiih the daring and outrageous acts of violence and rapine perpetrated by an infuriated Mob

in the early part of August last, has most materially lightened our labors, and we trust has served to dispel the feeling which a few disaflected individuals, whose position and pretences ought to have dictated an opposite course of proceeding, have sought to disseminate among the lower orders of society, viz : þÿ that the authorities were not justified ih endeavouring to repel, as (hey did, the unlawful aggression of the mob on the occasion of the riot. bully concurring with Your Honors, that not the least deplorable of the results of the outrages committed by the rioters, is our having been deprived on this occasion of the able assistance of our respected Chief Justice ; and duly appreciating the high principle which induced him to abstain from silting in judgment on those by whom he has been most wantonly and undeservedly injured, we have derived much satisfaction from the fact that the Court is so constituted as to deprive the most cavilling objector of just complaint. The high reputation which you Mr. I'resident have earned from your able and impartial administration of the Law in the Island of St Kit is. is too well known to require comment Irom us ; and in your presence it might be unbecoming in us to oiler any þÿ but we cannot retrain from expressing our tribute ol respect to His Excellency the Governor-General, for the benignant feeling towards those who Were to be tried, evinced in the selection of Your Honor to preside upon their trials. Unconnected with the Colony by any local

tics, either of interest in property or relationship wiih any ol its inhabitants, Your Honor cannot be suspected of undue bias or prejudice. And your Honors, his associates, having fortunately escaped injury at the hands of the unhappy individuals, whose judges you are (except in so lar as you shared in the general calamity) are unexceptionable in this respect, while your competency from position and character is indispensable. Thus a tribunal has been formed, which in every point of view secures to the accused a fair, honest, and impartial consideration of the charges by which they may stand affected. The causes and circumstances which evented in such deplorable results as stated byjyour President, do not very clearly appear. From ruinour, we have learned that a strong objection to the increased Cattle Tax existed among a portion of the labouring population. We have reason however to believe, from our knowledge of many of them, that their dislike to the impost wotrld, in all probability, have passed away in murmurs of discontent, and would never have burst forth into the desolating storm which ensued ; but for the w il v suggestions of some evil disposed persons who readily seized the opportunity to incite the ignorant and easily deluded to resist the I, aw, and created an amount of disaffection which eventually manifested itself in open acts of violence and a fearful destruction of property. INTELLIGENCE from SI. Thomas. By an official account from St. Thomas of the 19th instant we learn that, the mortality there had been on the increase, as up to that day there had been altogether 20 fatal cases of the same symptoms as those which characterised the epidemic that broke out on the Estate Hull. Of these 12 died on this estate, 1 on the estate Caretbay, 2 on Crown, 1 on Niesky and 4 in the town. It was however discovered that they all, with the exception of one the cause of whose death was uncertain, had been on the estate shortly before, from whieli circumstance it was presumed that the epidemic is attributable to a local cause. The first person attacked was the fisherman of tlie estate, who bad boon aboard the Emigrant Sliip Atlas, wrecked on the Northside of the Island ; but among that mass of persons who were aboard that ship, no disease prevailed, not even after their arrival at St. Thomas. The strong northerly wind which prevailed a few days previously had caused an uncommon high tide, which had thrown up a quantity of fish on the beach þÿ of which the people denied to have eaten. It also swamped a cane piece of low land, and filled the well situated on the beach. The people ascribe the disease to the mixing of the salt water with the well water which they drank, and also to their having eaten of the canes from the swamped cane piece.- By a chemical analysis of the well water no metallic poison lias been detected, but it contained salt in solution. The

analysis of the canes lias likewise not led to any satisfactory result. From the symptoms of the disease the King's Physician and several other Doctors have arrived at this result, that they consider it to lie Cholera ; and from a post mortem examination of two of the bodies this opinion has been confirmed. An official report of the 20tli, which has since come to hand, states that up to the time of its despatch (half past 4 o'clock in the afternoon) no fresh cases of the epidemic has been reported ; which lias led the authorities to entertain the hope that the disease, notwithstanding its symptoms, is not really Cholera ; but was of a local and transient nature. On the part of Government, all vessels from St. Thomas and the circumjacent Islands are placed under quarantine ; and the Government Schooner Vigilant was despatched on the 21st to St. Thomas to obtain further intelligence as to whether the disease is on the increase, or, as we should hope, on the decrease. The captain of a boat, which arrived at Frederikstcd the day before yesterday from St. Eustatius, states that Cholera has not extended farther than Nevis, owing to the strict precautions adopted by the Government, to prevent any communication with that place. The intercourse carried on is by boats, which do not come nearer each other than to be hailed for intelligence, which is to this effect : that out of a small population 80 persons have died in 14 days, from which number 12 or 14 died on the last day, and

further, that the disease was on the increase. I'Tirllin Intelligence. The Government Schooner Vigilant arrived here last night from St. Thomas and brought an official report of yesterday's date stating that 13

new cases had been reported up to yesterday afternoon ; and that 0 of this number proved fatal. Of these eases 0 were ou the Estate Hull, of which 3 died ; 1 died on the Estate Musquito Bay, which person, it is however to be observed, had been a few days previously on the Estate llull ; 4 cases in town, out of which 2 fatal ; none of these persons had had the least communication with the latter Estate, and lastly 2 French sailors. The disease is declared by the King's Physician as well as by the other Doctors to have all the symptoms of Cholera. <<- We c5 give 1 he resu of the late elections for Members of the Colonial Assembly : Foe Clirisliansled's District, W. GOHHIAHATiOA. Mr. Editor, Allow me through the medium of your Paper, to make a proposition, which I am sure will be responded to by every one. As that awful pestilence, the Cholera, is now hovering near the shores of our beloved little Island, and as its exterminating effects in the West Indies are too well known from its recent visitations to some of the larger neighboring (slauds, and judging from these what its consequences in this small community would be, as well in its social, as in its general bearing þÿ knowing also that the best sanitary regulations although they may tend to diminish its virulence, cannot, ward it off, let us as a community, cast ourselves on the mercy of Almighty God, and by way of showing that we acknowledge him to be the Ruler of all events, and the God in whose hand our breath is, let there be a day appointed as a general fast throughout the Island, for humiliation and prayer, and it may be with us as it was with the Niuevitcs of old when they repented in sackcloth and ashes, the hand of the destroying Angel was stayed, and they were spared.

From the Diario de Avisos, Carinas, 2<D/t November 1853. FOREIGN EG AltlS. Our foreign relations are assuming a very disagreeable aspect. We were informed several days ago, that the English legation kept urging the payment of the interest of the English debt in conformity with the stipulations for the present year, amounting according to the statement published, to $547,959 ; besides, the sum of one million and a half dollars, due as arrears. The public reports in circulation announce that Air. Bingham exacts firstly, the fulfilment of the 6th article of the Legislative Decree of 1851 which ordains the exclusive application of the total of the receipts of' the extraordinary tax. We understand that this amount has been disposed of by the Executive with the sanction of the Council of Government consulted to that effect, and in conformity with the desire of several of the administrators of the Customs, to obtain especial power in regard of the matter to satisfy urgent demands, independent of the stipulated purpose. These circumstances will without doubt cause some embarrassment to the Executive. On the other hand Senor Vera the Spanish Charge I)' Affaires, strenuously urges the payment of the claims of Espera : and, towards the liquidation of the interest and gradual reduction of the capital, he assigns a necessary, the payment of one hundred thousand dollars Until

this moment he has not been able to obtain a decision in accordance with the amount which he , claims in a very pressing manner. The business appears to have assumed a grave character ; to that extent as to have caused the Spanish Minister to demand his passport, if not justly satisfied. We will be careful in informing our readers of the progress and result ot this affair peaceable, undoubtedly, as usual in similar þÿcases whenever wo obtain . . such information as to establish # # an opinion. (Concluded) More than one public meeting was held about two months before the outbreak, attended by large numbers of the people; and however cautious the language addressed to them mav have been, we have reason to know that the speakers were understood by some at least of those present, to have addressed them in opposition to the 1 axes which bore upon them as a class ; and irrespectively of this fact, we conceive that those who convened and took part in such meetings incurred a serious responsibility by assembling in large numbers ignorant persons whose minds were in an unsettled state on the subject ol taxation generally. 'The natural tendency of such meetings under such circumstances, was undoubtedly hazardous to social order, and too fatally has the result vindicated the correctness of what might have been predicated in regard to them. It is to be hoped that the promoters of these meetings have learned, when too late, what slight reflection would have pointed out in the first instance, the fatal consequences to use your President's forcible þÿexpression of handling edged tools. We would guard ourselves against being supposed to deny to any of our fellow-Cilizens, the right of free discussion on matters which concern the public generally, or any class in particular þÿ far less to deprive them of the privilege of petitioning against any legislative enactment, which may seem to those concerned to bear with unnecessary weight upon them, but we do assert that to address a crowded auditory of the poorer

and ignorant classes, at a lime, when, with minds heated and distempered, they are brooding over wrongs whether real or imaginary, is to employ an agency unnecessary for the purpose of legitimate redress, and the employment of which can never be justified in religion and morality. We concur with the Court in the opinion expressed by the President as to the duty of those who, by their calling, or the natural bent of their feelings, are most sensitively alive to the interest of the labouring population ; but we regret to add that it appears to usmst certain, that sofarfrom enjoining upon their followers a deferential reliance on the sense of justice of the Legislature, and the paternal vigilance of the Executive, the pretended friends of these ignorant individuals have too often by incidental expressions, if not by direct incitement, inculcated a spirit of hostility to lawful authority and constitutional Government. The practice alluded to by your President so prevalent in small communities, and so baneful to the best interests of society þÿ of

fj J I 3£ A T 1 3. commenting in unmeasured terms on the proceedings of the legislative bodies, has, we fear, been of late fatally resorted to, in reference to the Legislative bodies of these Islands ; and though we are aware that they require no vindication and can deiive no support from us, yet, as the subject has been thus brought casually to our notice, in your Honor's address, we woiild take leave to remark that, as far as we can judge, the particular tax so much complained of þÿ and so loudly condemned by those who profess to be sensitively alive to the interests ol the labouring population, was not only fully justifiable in view of the value ol the object assessed, but absolutely necessary in the existing circumstances ol the Colony- A reference to the present system and scale of taxation will clearly demonstrate to all but the wilfully, or selfishly blind, that no other species of property could so well have borne an augmented impost as Cattle; which always command a ready sale ami a lair price in the neighbouring Island of St. V þÿIro mas. Referring to this lact þÿ aware that the Agricultural population have an unlimited liberty of pasturage on the Lands ol others, without any exaction for the exercise of it ; and urgently and repeatedly pressed by the Executive, as we are inlormed, to make some immediate provision for the repairs ot the Court House, Jail, and Poor House. 1 he Legislature wisely and ightlv. i in our estimation, imposed the tax mentioned lor this specific, purpose ; and we conceive that it any

justification ol the tax was requited it would be found in this its appreciation. I o render fit for public use the Court House, which the in labouring classes have an equal privilege and the same opportunity with every other class to asseit their rights against the wrong doer and the oppressor ; to secure and render habitable the Jail, where oflenders against their fellow-Citizens or the community, must atone for their aggressions upon private rights ; and expiate the crimes which in their nature affect society at large ; and to repair the Poor House, which affords shelter to the indigent, the infirm, and the afflicted þÿ were surely matters of import to the lower orders, and may be held to concern them in an especial degree. Indeed it is hardly too much to say that a tax paid by them for such purposes, bears the character of a contribution to a Benefit Society. While we have thus ventured to give expression to our opinion on the foregoing subjects, casually noticed by your President, or suggested by what fell from him, we trust we have not in our investigation lost sight of the caution, that a consideration ol the causes of the disturbances formed no part of our duly while deliberating on the respective chaiges against particular individuals, and that while so engaged, we have strictly confined our attention to the points themselves without reference to what led to them. We again beg to thank your Honor lor the able and lucid explanation of the law, afforded us in your President's charge ; without

winch we could not have dealt properly with the Gases submitted to us ; and in readily receiving and rigidly adhering to which, we have at once discharged a duty and reaped an advantage. GEORGE HENRY MAR UN. toreman.
DEATH OP THE QUEEN OP PORTUGAL Intelligence was received on Sunday at the

Portuguese legation of the death ot her Majesty the Queen of Portugal, who died in childbirth on the 15th inst., at noon. The infant, a prince, did not survive. By the death of Donna Maria da Gloria, Queen of Portugal, the Crown of that ancient kingdom has devolved on her son, Don Pedro, a prince who has not yet attained liis majority, having barely completed the 16th year of his age. It is stated that the King-Consort at once assumed the Regency in the name of his son, the present King of Portugal. The minority of the young king, Pedro V., will terminate in Sept. 1855. Although the late Queen was still young, having been born on the 4tli of April, 1819, only a month before her Majesty Queen Victoria, her name belongs to transactions and contests which have long passed away. Her life especially in her earliest years, was singularly agitated and unfortunate ; and the subsequent period of her reign has not responded to the enthusiastic hopes of the Constitutional party which placed her on the throne. Her political career may be said to have begun in her infancy, for she was still at llio Janeiro, the place of her birth, in 1826, when the death of King John IV., followed by the renunciation of the crown by her father and the proclamation of the Constitutional Charter raised her to the throne, and she was betrothed a few months afterwards to her uncle Don Miguel, then made Regent of the kingdom. No sooner, however, had this prince assumed the reins of government in the name of his niece than he

usurped the crown, and his first act was to forbid his Sovereign and his bride from landing in her own dominions. Donna Maria then came to England, where she was received by George IV., as lawful Queen of Portugal, and the leaders of the Constitutional party prepared for that struggle which they ultimately led to a successful issue with the assistance of the other members of the Quadruple Alliance. During that contest the young Queen resided in Brazil or in Paris, and it was not till Don Pedro had captured Lisbon that she was enabled, in September, 1833, to enter her capital and ascend her throne. Her father, unhappily, survived this event but one year, and on the 18th of September, 1834, the Cortes were induced unanimously to declare their sovereign, then only 15, to be of full age, and in complete possession of her royal prerogative. A few months later she contracted a marriage with Prince Augustus of' Leuchtenberg, the eldest son of Princo Eugene Bcauharnais ; but here again the singular ill-fortune of her life prevailed, and the Queen, married in January 1835, was a widow before Easter. A second marriage was concluded iu the following year with Prince Ferdinand, of the Catholic branch of the Coburg family, which has conferred upon the house þÿ of Braganza no less than eight lineal descendants Observer, November 27

The Cholera having made its appearance in St. Thomas and other Islands, it is hereby ordered with a view to prevent infection in the country districts of St. Croix : 1, Houses and outbuildings thereto belonging shall be kept strictly clean by the occupiers thereof; no weeds shall bo allowed to grow, and no filth or garbage or dirty water shall be thrown or be suffered to remain within a distance of twenty feet from any house, or within the villages. 2, The laborers' houses and any other dwellings of similar description shall bo forthwith whitewashed inside, and if of wall outside. 3, No hogpens shall bo allowed to remain near to any bouse, nor in any village, but forthwith be removed to a convenient distance, and, wherever practicable to leeward. Also horsestables shall be removed from the villages, wherever considered offensive. 4, Until f urther order no public nor joint parties, or dances, at which any spirituous liquors are used or distributed, shall be permitted after nightfall. 5, Any case of sudden or suspicious illness, particularly if accompanied with vomiting and bad bowels, shall be reported forthwith to the manager or other person iu authority on the estate, and by him to the police. ti, Managers of estates shall do the needful to see the above rules complied with, and report any contraventions to the police. They are also requested to explain to the laborers and other persons residing on the estates the urgent necessity of temperance and cleanliness.

7, The present order, which will be distributed through the country, shall be acted on immediately, the police of each jurisdiction shall control the execution thereof and cause any offenders to be brought to justice.
