1' R EC A li IT O A A R V RLE E S to lie attended to for obviating the Cholera Epidemic.

1. Not to dwell or stay in places with confined, impure, and damp air; all habitations must be frequently aired and the apartments daily ventilated by opening the windows. Everything should be removed that can in any way engender obnoxious exhalations ; perfect cleanliness inside as well as outside the houses must be strictly attended to ; all houses and apartments with confined air or that have not always been kept perfectly clean, to be white washed inside. 2. Exposure which may lead to taking cold should be guarded against by avoiding sudden change from beat to eold, by properclothing, and by changing damp or wet clot lies as soon as possible. A belt of warm stufi, worn round the stomach, and warm clothes next to the skin, so as to produce mild perspiration, is also very beneficial. 3. Cleanliness must be strictly attended to, as well as regards linen apparel and sheets, as with respect to bathing and washing the body. 4. All continued excitement, dejection of mind, as well as nervousness and fear, sitting up at night and every thing that enfeebles the body must be avoided. 5'. Temperance in eating and drinking must be observed strictly. Want of food as well as excess and bad quality has a pernicious influence. Eating all kinds of indigestible, sour, fat, flatulent and purgative food, such as raw, especially unripe fruit and vegetables, melons, cucumbers, cabbage, and turnips, the fat of pork, fat fish, tainted meat and fish, &c., must be avoided. It is beneficial to add a proper quantity of

spices in the cooked victuals. As regards drinkables, the following must be especially avoided: bad water, sour beer, curdled milk and the use of spirituous liquors ; þÿ a small quantity of the last mentioned article mixed with spicy and bitter substances will however not injure

those accustomed to the use thereof; good wine used moderately may also be allowed. Generally speaking it. is best to continue the habitual diet, in so far as that be not in opposition to what is stated above.

þÿ « þÿ D I R I : c T IONS for attending to the symptoms of the CHOLERA and the treatment of the ease previous to medical aid being obtained. The Cholera comes on either suddenly, or after a patient has for some time felt unwell and has suffered from debility, restlessness, heaviness of the bead, gid dincss, oppression in the pit of the heart, dislike to food, nausea, vomiting, and þÿ almost always þÿ diarrhea either with or without griping, and spasms in the limbs. The sick person must immediately go to bed and be covered well, and against the diarrhea or griping in the stomach take 20 drops of Camphor drops, Hoffmann's drops, or Peppermint, every hour, to be repeated several times, and frequently take warm draughts, f. i . , salep, soup made of rice, oat meal or barley, common tea or tea made of chamomile, of the elder-leaf or of peppermint, with admixture of a small quantity of wine or brandy. Perspiration being always beneficial, and in order to promote it the more, the patient may take Minder drops, (Spiritus Mindcreri,) according to the age, say from one teaspoonfnl to one tablespoonfull every second hour. Should the warm draughts be obnoxious to the patient, or increase the vomiting, then it may be very beneficial to give cold water, especially iced, say a glass every quart or half hour, mixed with Minder-spirits or camphor-drops. In case the diarrhea continues, then to a grown person may be given 10 to 20 drops of laudanum together with the camphor drops, and for Hie griping of

the stomach rubbing with thick camphor oil alone or mixed with about one sixth part of laudanum. The violent symptoms, that either come on suddenly or ensue after those milder ones stated above, are frequent and painless diarrhea, vomiting, great thirst, beat inwardly ; the breath as well as the tongue and the skin, especially on the bands and feet ice-cold, the skin shrunken, pale or bluish, often with cold sweat, the eyes, sunken with blue rings around them, the voice hoarse, the pulse weak, scarcely to be felt, stoppage of urine ; severe cramps come on at times in the pit of the abdomen, in the arms and the legs, dullness and indifference, 1 bough without loss of the senses, and often strength enough to walk even shortly before death. The evacuations from vomiting and diarrhea may at the commencement be bilious, but aftcrwardsconsist of a limpid or mucous humour somewhat like thin oat meal soup or rice water. In these cases must be applied, besides the means already mentioned, frictionwith the bands, with flesh brushes or woollen cloth dipped into brandy mixed with salt and black pepper (a spoonful of each), or dipped in spirits of camphor or oil ofturpentine ; þÿ where the skin is most cold a jug of warm water, or bags with heated sand or ashes should be laid on ; þÿ on the arms, the calf of the legs and the heart, mustard plaisters þÿ (mustard stirred in warm water or vinegar laid between linen) þÿ must be applied, and be removed alter 15-20 min-

3 5 utes, and soon after be renewed ; the great thirst and vomiting are often checked by ice-cold water, or by swallowing small pieces of ice, but seldom the patient feels better from lukewarm draughts. In case of rushing of the blood to the head attended with great drowsiness and heaviness, cold applications must be used to be renewed every 4 or 5 minutes, and 0 or 8 leeches must be applied to the temples. The severe cramps are relieved in the best manner by rubbing with oil of camphor mixed, as before mentioned, with laudanum. As the disease is the more readily removed the earlier the means are applied, it is advisable to be furnished with some of them, especially laudanum, thick oil of camphor, chamomile flowers or elderleaves, mustard, brandy, and black pepper. f f The following precautions against the Cholera were i sued by t lie Hoard of Health in St. Christopher, on the Dth of I )ecemher 1853. First Sustrueiioii. Guard against Looseness of Bowels ami V urging. Malignant Cholera generally comes on with some purging or looseness of the bowels. The lirst measure to be taken should be, to apply for advice to the nearest practitioner of medicine, who will afford to poor persons or those in straitened circumstances such advice at the publie expense. The person so attacked with purging should go to bed at once, and take immediately thirty drops of laudanum in some warm ginger or other tea, and cover himself or herself with warm clothing. If medical advice cannot be procured immediately, and the purging continues, from 8 to I '2 drops of laudanum may be taken every two or three hours. Second Instruction. IVlull is to be i tone if a person is seized or !al%en with Cholera. If there is coldness of the hands or feet, bottles of warm water, heated bricks, or bags filled with hot sand should be applied to the soles of the feet, the insides of the thighs, and to the palms of the hands, and to the arm pits. Flannel warmed by heated irons or diplied in hot water þÿ or mustard poultices þÿ may be applied over the chest and bowels þÿ and a wineglassful of hot brandy and water may be taken every two hours or so. Third I nsf ruction. ( hi Food. All kinds of fruits, salads, cucumbers, spinach, and pickles had better by avoided ; also ovsters, crabs, muscles, or other

shell fish. The most wholesome articles of food are well baked bread, good biscuits, rice, oatmeal, and good tlrv potatoes; solid food is better than fluid. Fourlli Instruction. (hi Hie danger of Spirits, I hi in, Beer, fe. It is a very common notion that brandy, whiskey, rum, wine, and the like, are good as a protection against the Cholera. This is a total and fatal mistake; in every country and town where the Cholera has broken out, drunkards, and those who drink freely, have been the first and greatest sufferers from the disease; temperate persons usually escape, drunkards usually die.

C D I AT Jt £ Fifth instruction. Against exposure to IVet and Cold. Wet and cold, and especially wet or damp feet should as much as possible be i guarded against, over sudden changes of temperature and currents airshould ot be avoided. Sixth Instruction. Coneerning Cleanliness and f eiitilatioii. Nothing is of greater importance as a protection against Cholera, than cleanliness, and a good supply of fresh pure air. It is, therefore, indispensable to remove all filth from and around dwellings ; to lime-wash living and sleeping apartments; to admit freely pure air; and especially to guard against overcrowding. European experience has confirmed the experience of India, that Cholera is not contagious. There is no danger from infected persons; the true danger is continuing to live in infected districts in close, damp, and filthy dwellings. þÿ «"COcc-"- Fromthe Si. Thomas Times, Pee. 21, 1853.

The Inhabitants of this Island were on Saturday morning last startled from their accustomed as fire laborers of the Estate quietude by the disagreeable " report that as many Eensomhcd," la tter known as " Hull," had been suddenly attacked with Diarrhoea and spasms of the 1 >ody , which terminated fatally after a few hours suffering, and that there were others continuing to he seized in the same manner, and that the result would be fatal. On enquiry being made of the King's Physician, Doctor Ericiiso.n, who bad visited the estate on Friday night, to elicit some explanation as to the causes which could have produced so sudden a malady, that gentleman, we are informed, stated on Saturday morning that the time was too brief to enable him with anything like accuracy to decide as to the causes, hut that the disease of which the patients had died, and those that were dying, was the premonitory symptoms of Cholera ; but that nevertheless it could so happen that the sickness arose from circumstances solely confined to the estate, and the patients who bad been attacked. Later in the day (Saturday) the news from the estate continuing less satisfactory, the Burgher Council desired the King's Physician to select two more of the Faculty and proceed to the estate, and endeavor to ascertain by a closer examination the origin c A' the disorder, so as to allay if possible unnecessary alarm, or if the disease proved to bo Cholera, whether of a severe or mild type, timely sanitary precautions eould be

adopted to suppress, as tar as human efforts go, its spread or increase. The conclusions arrived at by these professional gentlemen during their consultations were to the effect, that, the symptoms of the disease the patients had died of were those of Cholera ; hut that there were local circumstances connected with the estate that called for much consideration. These causes we will now briefly review : þÿ During the end of the last and in the early part of the present month, the North West part of this Island, where Hull is situated, was visited with a terrible rising of the sea þÿ generally termed by fishermen a " ground swell" þÿ during which it rose to an unusual height, evidenced by lodgments of moss and sea-weed found on the rocks along the cliffs at an elevation of thirty-five feet above the ordinary tide. During this "ground-swell" the sea washed inland many hundred yards, and is supposed to have done much more so in the level land ol Hull estate ; in this way large pools of salt water were formed among the canes in the valley, as well as tilling many of the wells therein situated 'I his water after a while becoming stagnant, unwholesome matter may possibly have collected in and

about it, and that even the canes during their ' growth may have been affected by the same þÿ a supposition wo are told by no means unreasonable, inasmuch as it is reported that the canes in the vicinity just before being cut exhibited evidences of blithe, and these, we understand, were the canes that, were in process of grinding when the sickness broke out, and as a common custom, no doubt the laborers had been drinking freely of the liquor. In like manner, quantities of sea spray may have passed over the estate, and to a certain extent injured the Provisions in the negro grounds, and on being used acted as poison to the human stomach. On Sunday morning the number of deaths had increased to ten, the news causing the town population to grow further alarmed, as till then nothing was ascertained as to the real nature of the malady. The Commandant accordingly on that day convened a meeting at Government House of the entire corps of Medical men in this town, and Mr. A. II. 1'wise, Apothecary, in order that no measure calculated to maintain the health of the city should he overlooked. We believe, as tempora ry measures, it was there decided þÿ That the Cordon which had been established around the Estate " IIull" on the previous day should be continued with unremitting force : That the Inhabitants should be recommended to have about their persons pieces of Camphor, as the same had been found of infinite use iu Europe during a period of Cholera. That in the event of any death occurring with

in the city, the body should without delay be interred, without procession, or any other form used at funerals. That a Sanitary Hoard should he instituted, composed of three influential Burghers and three Physicians, who should from day to day meet and devise all means deemed advisable for the preservation of the public health This Board is composed of Major Wolff, 8 B. Langc, and C. G. Iletse, Esqrs. þÿ Doctors Erichson, Magens, and Cornucl þÿ and A. 11 Riise, Esqr., Apothecary. The advice given to the public with regard to Camphor appears to have been readily received, for during the aftern'oon of Sunday an immense quantity ol' that article was served out from the Apothecary Hall. We have thus far attempted to describe those incidents connected with the Estate which could have occasioned a malignant disease to break out there ; and we will also endeavour to shew what has resulted from the same. From Friday last, the IGtli instant, to the present time, there have been 1ft deaths in all at the estate Eensomhed ; no deaths have occurred in any other part of the country, or in Town, excepting those persons who in defiance of all advice during the first days persisted in going to the albrc-mcntioncd Estate, or had been there the day before the disease begun. The following is a list: þÿ a woman from the estate Caretbay, who, on returning home, was seized with the symptoms already described, and died a few hours after. A man and a woman from the estate Crown were attacked on reaching home,

and died shortly after. A woman from the estate Mosquito Bay returned home and died. Two men and one wowan who had gone from Town, died, and were buried on Sunday and Monday. From the foregoing our readers will perceive that no cases of death have as yet transpired in the Island, with symptoms of Cholera, but those which have had their origin at the estate IIull . and wo would, therefore, say, that it would be only a proper and prudent conclusion to arrive at. that there was no Cholera in the country, until it should unfortunately so happen that a ease occurs totally apart, unconnected, and having nothing to do with the estate Frnsnmhrtl

Publication. The Cholera having made its appearance in St. Thomas and other Islands, it is hereby ordered with a view to prevent infection in the country districts of St. Croix : 1, Houses and outbuildings thereto belonging shall be kept strictly clean by the occupiers thereof ; no weeds shall be allowed to grow, and no filth or garbage or dirty water shall be thrown or be suffered to remain within a distance of twenty feet from any house, or within the villages. þÿ 2, The laborers' houses and any other dwellings of similar description shall be forthwith whitewashed inside, and if of wall outside. 3, No hogpens shall be allowed to remain near to any house, nor in any village, but forthwith be removed to a convenient distance, and, wherever practicable to leeward. Also horsestables shall be removed from the villages, wherever considered offensive. 4, Until further order no public or joint parties, nor dances, at which any spirituous liquors are used or distributed, shall be permitted after nightfall. 5, Any case of sudden or suspicious illness, particularly if accompanied with vomiting and bad bowels, shall be reported forthwith to the manager or other person in authority on the estate, and by him to the police. 6, Managers of estates shall do the needful to see the above rules complied with, and report any contraventions to the police. They arc also requested to explain to the laborers and other persons residing on the estates the urgent necessity of temperance and cleanliness.

7, The present order, which will be distributed through the country, shall be acted on immediately, the police of each jurisdiction shall control the execution thereof and cause any offenders to be brought to justice. We copy tbe following distressing account of tbe mortality in St. Thomas: From the St. Thomas Times, Dee. 28, 1853.

The Cholera ! ! ! When on tbe 21st instant we adverted out on tbe estate " Eensomhed," we un- to tbe malignant disease that bad broken dertook to express a cheering doubt whether it would prove to be Cholera ; that doubt, with a too melancholy and direful effect, has since been entirely removed, and alas it is our painful duty now to chronicle the appearance in this Island of confirmed ASIA TIC CHO- LERA, of tbe most destructive type, and as dreadful in its progress as any plague or disease that we have ever known or beard of, and more surpassing in its deadly grasp upon tbe human family here that any distemper or pest that was ever known since tbe Island was civilized, or discovered. With us the victims are those who seemingly are tbe victims of all other countries, viz., tbe unfortunate individuals at the very bottom of the social scale ; and upon these the scourge seems invariably to spit its most bitter and unremitting venom. As may lie conceived, the community of this Island has never before in its annals lived tbrongb so distressing, exciting, and alarming an epoch, þÿ and may it be tbe kind will of an all-wise Providence to reduce it to its shortest span, for in five days we have been living as it were through an age, the mortality of which has caused the stoutest heart to shudder and sicken. We shall not in t his part of our notice attempt to recapitulate the deaths that have taken place during Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, as we can enter on that topic at the close of our

afflicting article þÿ preferring to detail, however imperfectly, the prompt and invaluable measures adopted and pursued by the Authorities to prepare the way to hold down, it possible, the spread of the scourge; and although it is not in our power to (ore-say withwhat success, yet all must agree with ns that however bad or desperate tilings have been, alacrity on the part of the Government has much subdued what would otherwise have been worse; yet we still further hope "that prevention is now usurping the place of cure. We mentioned in an earlier number that llis Honor the Commandant had instituted a Sanitary Board, or Board of Health, which in accordance with the appointment has been holding its sittings daily at the residence of this M r. Board A timely measure of A. II. Ruse. was to divide the town into six districts and to nominate a Physician to each, in order

that tlit! poorer classes should receive medical aid ; and the Board also proposed to the Burgher Council þÿ which proposition that Body acceded to þÿ to appoint Four citizens to each district, whose duty it would be to acquaint themselves of the wants and necessities of the people situated in their respective quarters; these gentlemen, we have every reason to believe, have with praiseworthy promptitude and exertion performed the duties assigned to them. The Cholera first shewing itself in the valley known to us as the "Back-of-All," a Dispensary was immediately opened in the Market Place, where Medicines, Blankets, and Brandy, have been freely distributed; and with a further desire to deprive the disease of material to feed on, the Commandant caused Tents to be erected with all possible speed classes from the " Back-of-All" were re- beyond the Town, where the humbler commended to camp out ; and our surprise is at seeing the immense quantity of work which was necessary to be done accomplished in so brief a time. We shall pass over with as little notice as possible that part of our narrative which embodies the most piercing and heart rending of all and relates to the deaths, and the precipitance with which the interments have of necessity to he gone through with. It is enough to know that these are scenes which will unhappily long live in the recollection of all who have taken part in, or witnessed, tlieni. To consign daily to their last resting place an average of SIXTY'

hum an beings must demand tact, ability, and unswerving perseverance from those whose position it is to direct. Another sanitary measure which we conceive to be of infinite use is that of fumigating the Town, which commenced 011 Sunday forenoon, and has to the present time been continued. The medicines that have been dispensed within a week from the Apothecary Hall are beyond the limits of calculation, which, in tiie words of a gentleman, with whom we have spoken, was enough in one day to absorb the entire stock of any similar Establishment in the YVest Indies. Where all are cheerfully performing the arduous tasks assigned to them, it would in one sense be wrong to allude to any particular individual but we þÿ hope to he pardoned lor exceptional cases that we may undertake to point out, and in doing so we shall venture to deviate from the hard beaten track by passing over those whose exalted stations must necessarily lead us to comprehend have left no stone unturned to mitigate the horrors ofour present position, i and address a few words to those who we believe deservedly merit them we þÿ shall then say that all praise is due to every individual member of our present Police Staff, whose duties have been of a most trying nature ; and foremost is that faithful old servant Brixen, whose services we hope at a becoming time will not fail to receive the public expression þÿ a man whose constitution seems adequate to beat down fatigue, and whose will seems capable to master dif-

ficulty; indeed there is but one Brixen in/uir community ! The following is a correct statement ol the mortality in the town : Saturday, 24th, 24. Sunday, 25th, 02. Monday, 26th, 0(1. Tuesday, 27th, 35. Wednesday, 28tli, (noon) II. Total 102.

COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, I suppose that the most incredulous individual among us 110 longer douhts that (Jholera, in a formidable shape, exists in these Islands ; that the terrible guest is, indeed, next door to us, whether naturally engendered by atmospheric influence or imported, 1 am not positively informed ; nor would I, for a moment, suppose that the most selfish and callous will deny that the time which may bo allowed us before our turn shall have come þÿ as come it will, I am persuaded, sooner or later þÿ should be turned to the best account in making preparations for his visit. Your recommendation of cleanliness, þÿ which the Christian proverb says is next to godliness, and temperance in meat and drink, þÿ with a free use of whitewash, and the use of free ventilation comes in very opportune, and if duly attended to, will be proved, as it has been found in other places to check, at least, the virulence of the disease. I am also glad to learn that the Quarantine laws have been revived, and only hope that they will be diligently and rigidly carried out, not only by day-light but during the night also. The sanitary commission is also very busy, and from personal observation of the zeal of the officers, I have no doubt that the town will soon be in a healthy condition þÿ although 1 have not yet heard of the banishmeut of the pigs, whose name in Frederiksted is legion. All these measures are indispensably necessary, and it is impossible to calculate their good effects.

But, Mr. Editor, can nothing more be done ? Is there anything left undone ? All these precautious were promptly taken þÿ in England, for instance, when the nation was threatened with Cholera, and after all had been done that human prudence and foresight could suggest, the clemency of Heaven was invoked. The Government appointed a day for a national fast and supplication, and the incense of prayer arose simultaneously from a thousand altars ! Will any Christian man say that this is superstition ? Will he venture the opinion that it is altogether a matter of Quarantine, and Chloride of lime and soap and water In short, the matter may be briefly stated thus. The practice of prayer is founded on the assumption that the ltulcr of the Universe continually interposes his Providence in all the affairs of its ordinary government, in which, far as as our limited mental vision is permitted to scan, we are 'able to trace the chain of secondary causes. This is the Christian's belief. If it were not so, all I say is, that half the prayers we use would be irrational. For if to pray and not to work is the part of indolence and superstition, surely it is a false and puerile philosophy that bids us work and not pray The Christian does both þÿ orat rt ' God laborat þÿ answers and finds no difficulty in the belief that his prayers through those very laws of i nature which are, after all, but the visible modes of operation of the Divine hand. I am sir, your obdt. scrvt. H Fredcriksted, Christmas Eve, 1853. þÿ

MONDAY, 21st NOVEMBER, 1853. Elizabeth Rornney sworn þÿ lltnnw prisoner by sight, but not by name. I saw the prisoner on the 2nd of August, first coming

from the President's then in the yard of Mr. John Davis' house; it is opposite Mr. Matthew Richardson's house ; at this time the fire was sot ; he was there when the fire blazed at Mr. Davis' place ; has no doubt of that; immediately after the fire blazed up, he retired, and a few others with him, and others were taking up stones and breaking op glasses in the inner part of Mr. Davis' house; the fire was then burning; is quite sure of the prisoner ; I know him by his face ; he was to build a house for himself on the land bv the Governor's; it was on Wednesday he said this. Gross-examined þÿ He used his hands breaking the glasses ; it was about 2 or after I ; on that day we did not know the hour; some were standing up to see that no one should put out the fire, others were pounding up the glasses ; was not one of the rioters ; God forbid 1 should have been so engaged. I saw him again 011 Wednesday, when he said he was to build the house; they were discussing what they were to do if they could catch Mr. Davis; they were to tie him and throw him into the burning house. Mr. John Davis þÿsworn On the 2nd August 1 occupied a house immediately opposite to Mr. Richardson's; can't tell the hour it was burned ; this house was the properly ol Mr. William Davis, Senior. Mr. G. 11. A. Porter, Gol. Secretary, sworn þÿ Recollects 2nd August; saw the house occupied by Mr. John Davis on fire; I was on board a vessel endeavoring to make my escape from the fury of the rioters. I saw the tire when it first appeared and broke

through the roof of Davis' house ; it was between 3 and 4 o'clock ; at past 4 we drew away at the point of the reef to run down for St. Thomas. I am Colonial Secretary and Clerk of the Council ; the Virgin Islands are one Parish; no Acts have been passed to alter the Parish ; it is called the Parish of Saint George. Mr. Jos. G. Gordon, Provost Marshal þÿ There is only one Parish in this Island ; it is the Parish of St. George; no other Parish exists in these Islands.

Mr. Isaacs, Q. C., addressed the Jury þÿ Gentlemen, I have proved that the prisoner took the burning materials from one part and put it to another. It will be observed that the house having been previously set fire to could constitute no defence, for this reason, if none other were alleged the first setting might have been extinguished. The witness Thomas, though he says he had only seen the prisoner but once before, yet he says that when his friend Elias said " Pompey don't set fire," lie said 1 will, Mr. Davis shot me ; lie had a shot.iu his nose, and was wounded 111 his arm and side ; that independently of his setting fire, his proximity to Elias, assisting by his presence. Their Honors will tell you it is sufficient to establish the piisoner's guilt, even had he not set fire to other partsol the house. 1 have proved the house was Mr. Davis'. As to the ptoof of intent to injure, Their Honors will, without invading your province, tell you that law infers that a party who does a tiling wilfully docs it maliciously ; even though a witness swear that the prisoner had no intention to injure the party mentioned in the Indictment it would not avail ; the malice could be inferred from the nature ol the act.

W. Birch. Public a t i o n. The Cholera having made its appearance in St. Thomas and other Islands, it is hereby ordered with a view to prevent infection in the country districts of St. Croix : 1 , Houses and outbuildings thereto belonging shall be kept strictly clean by the occupiers thereof ; no weeds shall be allowed to grow, and no filth or garbage or dirty water shall be thrown or be suffered to remain within a distance of twenty feet from any house, or within the villages. 2, The þÿlaborers houses and any other dwellings of similar description shall be forthwith whitewashed inside, and if of wall outside. 3, No hogpens shall be allowed to remain near to any house, nor in any village, but forthwith be removed to a convenient distance, and, wherever practicable to leeward. Also horsestables shall be removed from the villages, wherever considered offensive. 4, Until further order no public or joint parties, nor dances, at which any spirituous liquors are used or distributed, shall be permitted after nightfall. 6, Any case of sudden or suspicious illness, particularly if accompanied with vomiting and bad bowels, shall be reported forthwith to the manager or other person in authority on the estate, and by him to the police. fi, Managers of estates shall do the needful to see the above rules complied with, and report any contraventions to the police. They are also requested to explain to the laborers and other persons residing on the estates the urgent necessity of temperance and cleanliness.

7, The present order, which will be distributed through the country, shall be acted on immediately, the police of each jurisdiction shall control the execution thereof and cause any offenders to be brought to justice. Government of the Danish Westindia Possessions, St. Croix, the 24th December 1863. FEDDERSEN.

W. BIRCH. Publication. Masters of vessels and boats, and passengers are hereby warned to comply strictly with the Regulations forbidding the landing either persons or goods at any other places than those authorized for such landing, viz: the wharves at Christiansted and at Frederiksted, or communicating with shore before the harbormaster or the proper quarantine officers have granted leave. By the violation of those Regulations criminal responsibility is incurred, from whatever place the vessel may be coming, for the parties and for their accomplices ; if the vessel arrive from a place actually infected, capital punishment may be incurred. Quarter Officers, as well as others residing near the sea-coast, are hereby charged to prevent all illegal landing, and to report to the police all transgressions which may come to their knowledge. The inhabitants of towns and country are reminded of their duty to report strangers and persons who take up residence with them. Government of the Danish Westindia Possessions, St. Croix, the 27th of December 1853. Feddersen.

The want of change so much felt in this Island at present by those persons, who have small payments to make weekly, urges the question, why þÿdon people, t having already adopted the American computation of Dollars and Cents, make use of the American Silver pieces þÿ dimes and half dimes r We have heard it stated that the labourers in the country will not receive them, because shopkeepers in the towns will only receive dimes at the rate of five þÿstivers þÿpieces 6& cents. Should this prove to be correct, þÿ and we, by the by, learn that the American dimes, which some time ago were put in circulation, have been all bought up by speculators at the rate of 6j cents þÿ it follows naturally that no person, under such circumstances, will receive them for 10 cents, and give them out for 6$ Cents. We are informed that the Royal Treasurer receives dimes and half dimes in payments at their full value ; and in like manner dollars, half dollars, and quart dollars; consequently, when this is generally known, there will not. be room for speculation any longer. We expect therefore soon to sec dimes and half dimes freely circulated in this Island with our own money. Our remarks apply only to the small silver pieces, for as regards the copper cents, we scarcely think that they will find circulation in this Island ; although they are also received by the Royal Treasurer as payment to the State Treasury

OUR DUTY' TO THE SURVIVORS. Humanity, and the grateful sense of our preservation demands, that the earliest attention he given towards the relief of the aged surviving relatives, as well as the many orphans now destitute, and bereft of that support which they so lately derived from the victims ! We pronounce the task one of peculiar urgency, and moreover, do not entertain any doubts on the matter, -tinapprehension of infection did not prevent many noble minds to encounter CY'ery danger by personally administering medicines to the sufferers to the last moment. There are numbers who have given the brightest examples of their sympathy and fearlessness in behalf of the poor negroes. Merchants have, together with their clerks remained with the sufferers until death rendered all further efforts useless; nor is it necessary to linger on the merits of others, who have liberally contributed, either in a pecuniary manner, or by the furnishing of ample supplies of clothing or other necessaries, without having been in any manner solicited to do so, hut, in obedience to principles, which illustrate the sacred precepts : To do good indiscriminately þÿ to sow the seed nf benevolence so that others may reap the good example ! The greatest number of victims, from this sad visitation, resided in the overcrowded district occupied by the hulk of the Catholic population ; hence ; the extent of the responsibility, which so suddenly devolved on the llevd. Asm: Pratt, rendered its execution peculiarly arduous, as yvcII

as dangerous ; independent of the labour connected with the solemnities of the church at this season. Although unassisted, Mr. Pratt fulfilled his manifold duties witli zeal and the utter disregard of every personal consideration, by a continuous attendance on the sick and the dying ; and, moreover, in a worthy manner, upholding the moral confidence of the members of the Catholic community and others, by impressing on their mind, the necessity of faith and resign a tion to encounter the crisis allotted by Prnvi donee. However severe this calamity, the sooth ing reflection will long exist, that the sentiments of alarm did not stifle those of pity or individual firmness and exertions throughout the distressing scene which it has been our painful lot to witness in this community. We consequently anticipate that the duty, which yet remains to be performed, in regard to the survivors, especially the. orphans, will he faithfully accomplished.
St. Thomas, December 30th 1853

COMMUNICATIONS. For llic St. Croix Avis. There is, at present, a rumour afloat, that all communication between this island and St. Thomas is to be, for a time, suspended, as one of the means resorted to for the purpose of endeavouring to keep away the disease which pervades that island. There is no doubt but that this precaution, according to the circumstances of the case, is highly necessary ; and that it would be well to see to it in time. But here the ques- j Deaths from tion arises : Is there in this island a sufficiency of the necessaries of life to place us in a situation of temporary independence of the supplies to be obtained at that mart of commerce ? If so, good. But again, there are other questions of equal moment to be asked : Will merchants, shopkeepers and apothecaries vend their commodities at such a rate as to make the poorer class of people to support and medicate their bodies, in order to prevent, or else, mitigate the awful effects of Cholera ? Will extortionary speculation be discountenanced by all, and, consequently, practiced by none ? Will the desolating nature of this universally dreaded disease, even for a time, i temper down that speculative fever, which stimulates the business-man ? If so, then, again, I must say, good. In the midst of these considerations, however, I am compelled to pause ; for, , already is to be seen, a miniature exhibition of the reality of what we are to expect. A gradual rise is taking place in the price of provisions ; and such medicines as you may get at the Apo-

thecary Hall, you are compelled to pay well for. This state of things wears rather a gloomy aspect ; and seems to be the precursor of some very painful realities. A MALIGNANT DISEASE Having broken out in one, however, distant part of this Island, it is passible, that it may spread and reach the Town. It has been thought advisable to publish some general instructions, how best to guard against the sickness, and how to act before medical aid can be obtained. A strict CLEANLINESS ought to be observ ed. A LIGHT, and at the same time, WARM DRESS, should be worn, and Linen, Jc. changed often. The Dwelling-houses ought to be kept CLEAN, and if possible, white-washed ; all filth in and around them be removed ; the rooms ) properly AIRED with sufficient access of fresh pure air ; no overcrowding of the rooms must be allowed, and particularly not too many people the Houses will remain healthy, and their infection

Regarding FOOD : þÿ Everything ought to be avoided, that can produce looseness of the Bowels and Indigestion ; viz., Fruits, most Vegetables, (Salads, Peas, þÿ<f )> - Acids, and all Drinks that contain the same, þÿ likewise Beer j

Shellfish ; cold Preserved Meat, <$c. In Epidemics, habitual drinkers have the worst chance. The most whqlesome articles of Food are þÿ good Bread, Biscuits, Rice, Oatmeal, Sago, Arrowroot ; all kinds of Meat well prepared. Upon the whole Solids are better than Liquids. Tonics in moderate quantities are recommendable, as Aromatic Bitters and Port Wine. Moderate use of Rain-water or Iced-water, is not injurious. Exposure to Cold, and wet Feet, should be avoided. Steps have been taken to insure the public (particularly the poorer part thereof) Medical aid, by dividing the Town in districts and appointing Physician a to each. In every case of LOOSENESS BOWELS, of immediate application must be made to the Physician in the district, who will prescribe according to the case. But if by chance the þÿPhysician p s resence be required somewhere else, the sick must act in the following way : He must go to bed immediately and cover himself well up, and take, if a grown person, 15-25 drops of Laudanum (Tinct: opii spir:), and 30 Camphor drops (Liq: nervinus) in a cup of warm Tea, Camomile, Elderflower or Ginger Tea ; for Children, about 1 drop of Laudanum for every year of the þÿChild age. s This will, in most cases, stop the Looseness of the Bowels, and produce abundant perspiration, and the Sick be quite restored ; if not, 5-10 drops of Laudanum must be given every hour. Iu severer cases with coldness of Hands and Feet ; pains in the Stomach, and Vomiting; cramps in Legs and

Arms ; applications of warm Sand in bags, or hot Water in bottles, can be applied to Hands and Feet þÿ Mustard Poultices to the pit of the Stomach þÿ the Cramped extremities be rubbed mildly with warm Brandy, or Spirits of Camphor, (Spirit: vini campli:) either applied with a piece of Flannel, or the bare hand. A TOO FREE internal use of Camphor is injurious, as bad consequences have been seen viz , suppression of the þÿ Urine. St. Thomas, 10M December , 1853. ER1CHSON, þÿKing Physician. s CORNUEL. A. MUNICH, Dec 0 The demands of Austria are not confined to that of a strict neutrality to be observed by the Germanic Confederation on the Oriental question ; that neutrality is to have a certain character, and that character is to be determined by Austria. For this purpose secret negotiations have for some lime past been carried on at Munich by the agents of Saxony, Bavaria, and Austria. BELGRADE, Dec 3 The Porte has demanded of Servia, in the most categorical manner, the abandonment of its neutral position in favour of Turkey.

EXCERPT.® FROM THE LAST NEWS Prince VVoronzow, Commandcr-in-Chief of the Caucasus, is seriously ill at Tiflis. His embarrassed position is believed to have been the existing cause. The army of the Caucasus has been allowed to fall far below its disputed strength; as soon as its strength is put to the proof the truth is discovered, reinforcements are sent tor, but cannot arrive for a considerable time, if at all. Schamyl was threatening a descent upon the capital of Georgia itself. The Russian steam frigate Wladimir, cruising in the Black Sea, took the Bervass Bachri, an Egyptian war steamer of 10 guns, after an obstinate resistance. The captain of the latter is said to have been killed. The Russian lieutenant Gelezenoff also fell. The Russian war steamer Bessarabia has taken a Turkish steamer, laden with copper, belonging to Government. Both prizes were taken to Sebastopol. The official recall of the advertisement relativc to the supplies for the French fleet between Constantinople and þÿOdessa has caused a great sensation in Constantinople.

At the latest advices it was reported in the Turkish camp on the Danube that an exchange of prisoners having been talked of, the Russian prisoners had obtained an interview with Omar Pasha to beg him to keep them, as they could see his soldiers were much better treated than the Russian troops. It is added that Omar Pasha complied with their request, and incorporated them in the regiments now forming. The most recent letters from Kalisch state that two battering trains have been sent from Poland to the Principalities with small escorts, but of the second infantry corps now in Poland not one regiment has left the kingdom. Great activity reigns in the garrisons, and contracts for stores and provisions for this and that regiment are daily advertised in the public prints. General Uschakoff, director of Marshal þÿPaskiewitch chancery s has been sent on a special mission to Bucharest. Seventy-two Wallachian peasants have been sent prisoners to the Russian head quarters at Mazurelli, charged with having worked at the Turkish intrenchments at Oltenitza. A letter from the Polish frontier, dated Dec- 1, contains the following : þÿ At the commencement of winter in every year a general seizure of men required for military service takes place throughout Russian Poland ; and, under the name of the Branka, is universally dreaded. The day on which it takes place is one of horror and woe throughout the land. Seldom, indeed, does the unhappy conscript ever see his home again. In the course of

last week, that is to say, on the þÿ23 24th of November, (n Branka of this kind was executed throughout Russian Poland. The villages and hamlets which at other times have been called on to supply one or two men, have this time had to furnish eight and ten. The Branka is estimated at 50,000 þÿmen. Ibid.

COMMUNICATION. Mr. Editor, þÿ While perusing your last number, I read an article in which the health and economy of the community are advocated in a most able manner by " A Subscriber." It is seldom that we meet witli authors of this character ; men who stand forth so boldly in favour of health and economy, and support the same hv expressing their views through the medium of public opinion in spite of scorn. I have been led to admire the said article, because of the two-fold benefit which it offers to those who can duly appreciate the most liberal views advanced by its author. Now that cholera is so near our door, quarter, no doubt that the eating of " no and sooner orlater may pay a visit in this meat but that which is sound and good" may tend in some degree to act as a preventive to that most virulent diarrhea of the body, which is so strong and powerful, that it seldom fails to bring all to the commori level. This makes the suggestion of "A Subscriber," with regard to the eating of beef on the same day that the cattle is killed, of great importance. But the other point which appears so very striking in the article is the particular notice which he takes of the savings of the housekeeper. What a laudable subject ! take care of the cold pieces and you will nothavp to buy so many/resA

<0 m <© a AT1S ones ; this will certainly act as a good preventive to pocket diarrhea; an idea by those who know as well as " A Sub- which I hope will be readily understood scriber" does the benefits accruing to those who attend strictly to this matter. Whether the primary object of " A Subscriber" in offering the cattle-killing and sound-beef-eating hints be to effect a greater saving in the pantry and consequently save a little more in the pocket, by being able to make better use of the cold hits, or otherwise, I know not ; but whatever others may think of the matter, I think our author means well.
